page_hint: Ch 5 §3(b), first [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] paragraph and economics note
quoted_clause: vLLM continuous batching on 8×H100 with a 70B FP16 model and 9.2K context yields ~50 tokens/s aggregate throughput for 300‑token outputs.
observed: The same section later says 'the ~50 tok/s used here is a deliberately low-batch (single-stream) generation rate'. A single-stream decode rate cannot simultaneously be a continuous-batching aggregate throughput.
evidence: Direct textual contradiction within the same subsection: first paragraph labels 50 tok/s as continuous-batching aggregate; economics note labels it single-stream low-batch.
root_cause: Conflates single-stream decode rate with continuous-batching aggregate throughput.
correction: Label 50 tok/s consistently as a single-stream/low-batch decode rate. If a continuous-batching aggregate rate is intended, provide a separate batched rate and do not reuse 50 tok/s.
acceptance_test: Every occurrence of 50 tok/s is labeled single-stream/low-batch; no sentence calls it continuous-batching aggregate throughput.

quoted_clause: at ~50 tokens/s aggregate throughput ... 1.08 s prefill vs 7.5 s decode ... TPOT ~25 ms/token
observed: 50 tok/s corresponds to 20 ms/token, so 300 output tokens take 6.0 s, not 7.5 s. Conversely, 25 ms/token corresponds to 40 tok/s, so 300 tokens take 7.5 s. The section mixes 50 tok/s and 25 ms/token in the same worked example.
root_cause: Inconsistent canonical decode rate: 50 tok/s versus the canonical 25 ms/token (40 tok/s).
correction: Choose one decode rate for the worked example. If 25 ms/token is canonical, use 40 tok/s and recompute tokens/$ as 40×3600/20 = 7,200 tokens/$. If 50 tok/s is intended, use 20 ms/token and 6.0 s decode.
acceptance_test: All decode arithmetic in Ch 5 uses one rate; tokens/$ and wall-clock decode time are recomputed consistently.

page_hint: Ch 5 §3(b), 'tokens/s per dollar with prefill included' paragraph
quoted_clause: The same 9,000 tokens-per-dollar figure is a combined prefill+decode metric.
observed: 9,000 tokens/$ is computed from 50 output tok/s × 3600 ÷ $20. It counts output tokens only. If combined input+output tokens are intended, the total token rate for 9.2K input + 300 output is 50 × (1 + 9200/300) ≈ 1,583 tok/s, giving ≈285,000 tokens/$. If 50 tok/s is total token rate, output rate is ≈1.58 tok/s.
root_cause: Denominator/population error: output tokens versus total input+output tokens.
correction: Define the token basis explicitly. If 9,000 is output-token/$, call it that. If combined prefill+decode token economics are intended, include prefill tokens and recompute.
acceptance_test: The text states whether tokens/$ counts output tokens, input tokens, or total tokens, and the arithmetic matches that definition.

page_hint: Ch 5 §3(b), 'tokens/s per dollar with prefill included' paragraph
quoted_clause: prefill dominates the compute/FLOP budget (and hence the GPU-hour cost of running the pipeline)
observed: GPU-hour cost is wall-clock occupancy, not FLOP share. In the same example prefill is 1.08 s and decode is 7.5 s, so decode dominates per-request wall-clock. FLOP share cannot by itself establish GPU-hour cost share.
evidence: Prefill wall-clock share = 1.08/(1.08+7.5) ≈ 12.6%; decode share ≈ 87.4%. GPU-hours per request scale with wall-clock occupancy unless batching/occupancy changes the resource allocation.
root_cause: Conflates FLOP share with cost share.
correction: Separate FLOP share from GPU-hour share. State that prefill dominates linear FLOPs while decode dominates single-stream wall-clock; cost depends on batching, occupancy, and scheduling.
acceptance_test: No sentence infers GPU-hour cost directly from FLOP share; cost analysis uses time/occupancy or explicitly models batching.

page_hint: Ch 5 §3(b), 'tokens/s per dollar with prefill included' paragraph
quoted_clause: prefill is compute‑intensive yet batchable across concurrent requests, while decode is a sequentially‑limited token-by-token stream
observed: Decode is also batched across concurrent requests in continuous batching. The per-request token-by-token dependency remains, but that does not mean decode cannot be batched across requests.
evidence: Continuous batching explicitly batches decode steps from multiple requests; the text elsewhere relies on continuous batching.
root_cause: Conflates per-request sequential dependency with inability to batch across requests.
correction: Say decode has a per-request sequential dependency but can be batched across requests; batching improves GPU utilization without removing per-token latency.
acceptance_test: The text acknowledges decode batching across requests and does not imply decode is inherently non-batchable.

quoted_clause: Adding retrieval (~120 ms) puts the full TTFT (retrieval + prefill) at ~1.20 s, i.e. at the 1.2 s SLO line with no prefill-side margin; the real margin is the p95 ≤ 2 s target.
observed: 'Full TTFT' here includes only retrieval and prefill. It omits queueing, tokenization, network transit, scheduling, and first-token sampling. Also, 1.2 s was defined earlier as a TTFT budget, while the p95 SLO is ≤2 s; calling 1.2 s the 'SLO line' is terminology drift.
evidence: Earlier text: 'TTFT budget 1.2 s ... p95 TTFT ≤ 2 s'. The decomposition is retrieval + prefill only.
root_cause: Incomplete TTFT decomposition and inconsistent budget/SLO terminology.
correction: Call this a retrieval+prefill budget estimate, not 'full TTFT'. Either include the omitted TTFT components or explicitly scope them out. Use 'budget line' for 1.2 s and 'SLO' for the p95 target.
acceptance_test: TTFT decomposition labels all included and excluded components; 1.2 s is consistently called a budget, not an SLO.

page_hint: Ch 5 §3(a), decision paragraph after embedding table
quoted_clause: justify the 2×FLOP cost
observed: The table gives all-mpnet 14.08 GFLOP versus MiniLM 2.94 GFLOP, a ratio of 4.8×, not 2×. The 2× figure applies only to a same-family 384-dim versus 768-dim comparison, which is not the table comparison being discussed.
evidence: 14.08/2.94 = 4.79. The text itself says 'a same-family 384-dim variant is the ~2× case'.
root_cause: Mismatched comparison: cross-model all-mpnet vs MiniLM versus same-family dimension sweep.
correction: Use ~4.8× for all-mpnet vs MiniLM, or explicitly switch the sentence to the same-family 384 vs 768 comparison.
acceptance_test: The FLOP ratio in the decision sentence matches the table rows and the named comparison.

page_hint: Ch 5 §3(a), decision paragraph after embedding table
quoted_clause: (2 × params × L: 14.08 − 2.94 GFLOP, Table 5‑1's own rows; ...)
observed: Table 5-1 does not contain the 14.08 and 2.94 GFLOP rows. Those values are in the preceding embedding-model table, which is not Table 5-1.
evidence: Table 5-1 contains embedding dimension, model size, KV cost, tokens/$ and verdict; it does not contain per-embedding FLOPs.
root_cause: Wrong table cross-reference.
correction: Reference the embedding-model table by its actual number/caption, or add the FLOPs rows to Table 5-1.
acceptance_test: The cross-reference resolves to the table that actually contains 14.08 and 2.94 GFLOP.

quoted_clause: ~56–370 ms if encoded on a single CPU core at a realistic 30–200 GFLOP/s ... single-core encoding is the configuration that would not fit.
observed: At 200 GFLOP/s, 11.1 GFLOP takes 55.5 ms, which is within the ~120 ms retrieval budget. The statement that single-core encoding 'would not fit' is true only at the low end of the stated throughput range.
root_cause: Overgeneralizes from the upper end of the latency range.
correction: Say single-core encoding may not fit at the low end of single-core throughput, but can fit at the high end; make the conclusion conditional on measured throughput.
acceptance_test: The text states the throughput condition under which single-core encoding fits or does not fit.

quoted_clause: reducing the embedding dimension may trade retrieval quality for lower storage and compute — e.g. a 384‑dim variant of the same model family can cost roughly half the FLOPs and index storage of a 768‑dim one.
observed: Index storage scales with output dimension, but encoder FLOPs scale with model width, layer count, and parameter count, not output embedding dimension alone. A 384-dim output variant need not halve encoder FLOPs.
evidence: The FLOP formula 2×params×L depends on parameters, not output dimension. A model can have 768-dim output with the same encoder width as a 384-dim output variant.
root_cause: Conflates output embedding dimension with encoder model size.
correction: Distinguish output dimension from encoder width. Say index storage halves with D, while FLOPs halve only if the encoder itself is correspondingly smaller.
acceptance_test: The text separates storage scaling from compute scaling and does not attribute FLOP reduction to output dimension alone.

quoted_clause: The 24.1 GB KV cache for 9.2K input consumes ~4.8% of headroom, leaving ~475.9 GB for activations, intermediate buffers, and OS overhead.
observed: After the stated ~64 GB runtime reserve, the KV budget is ~436 GB. 24.1/436 ≈ 5.5%, leaving ~411.9 GB for other requests' KV. The 475.9 GB figure includes the 64 GB reserve and other requests' KV, not just activations/buffers/OS.
root_cause: Mixes pre-reserve headroom with post-reserve KV budget and mislabels the remainder.
correction: Use the 436 GB KV budget: 24.1 GB is ~5.5% of KV budget, leaving ~411.9 GB for other requests' KV; the 64 GB reserve covers activations/buffers/OS.
acceptance_test: The arithmetic and labels are consistent with the 436 GB KV budget and the 64 GB runtime reserve.

quoted_clause: the effective cost is ~0.40 $/tok/s, or equivalently ~2.5 tokens/s per dollar
observed: 50 tok/s ÷ $20/hr = 2.5 tok·hr/(s·$), not 2.5 tokens/s per dollar. The correct tokens-per-dollar figure is 50×3600/20 = 9,000 tokens/$.
evidence: Dimensional analysis: (tok/s)/($/hr) = tok·hr/(s·$); multiplying by 3600 s/hr gives tok/$.
root_cause: Unit error in the 'equivalently' clause.
correction: Remove 'equivalently' or express the intermediate as 2.5 (tok/s) per dollar-hour; keep 9,000 tokens/$ as the correct tokens-per-dollar figure.
acceptance_test: The units in the cost sentence are dimensionally consistent and the equivalence is correct.

quoted_clause: C_train is the one-time training compute ... value per corrected query
observed: The numerator must be currency for Q* to be a query count. 'Training compute' suggests FLOPs, not currency. The denominator uses ΔQ in corrected answers per query and 'value per corrected query'; the value term should be per corrected answer to cancel ΔQ.
evidence: Q* = (currency)/((answers/query)×(currency/answer)) = queries. If C_train is FLOPs or value is per query, the dimensions do not yield queries.
root_cause: Units and terminology not defined consistently.
correction: Define C_train as monetary training cost (including compute), and define the value term as value per corrected answer. State units explicitly.
acceptance_test: Dimensional analysis of Q* yields queries with the stated definitions.

quoted_clause: the base-model + RAG + guardrails paradigm is the economically preferred choice under this chapter's stated assumptions — the break-even ΔQ/Q of §3(c) is parametric here, not measured for this workload.
observed: If the break-even is parametric and not measured, the text has not established that RAG+guardrails is economically preferred. Also, 'ΔQ/Q' is not defined in the equation or surrounding text.
evidence: The preceding equation defines Q*, C_train, C_weights-extra, ΔQ, and value per corrected query; it does not define ΔQ/Q.
root_cause: Claim strength exceeds evidence and notation drift.
correction: Either provide a quantitative break-even calculation for the canonical workload or soften the claim to 'default under the stated assumptions; break-even not measured'. Define or remove ΔQ/Q.
acceptance_test: The takeaway's economic claim is supported by a calculation or explicitly labeled as an assumption; ΔQ/Q is defined or removed.

quoted_clause: The illustrative cloud-GPU training cost is presented as a scenario range, not a fact
observed: No cloud-GPU training-cost scenario range appears in the section. The sentence refers to content that is not present.
evidence: The chunk contains no training-cost range, only the parametric Q* equation and qualitative discussion.
root_cause: Dangling reference to missing content.
correction: Add the intended scenario range or remove the sentence claiming it is presented.
acceptance_test: The referenced scenario range exists in the section, or the sentence is removed.

quoted_clause: If the workload is input-heavy ... the system is memory‑capacity‑bound (KV residency) and prefill‑dominated — prefill itself sits in the compute‑bound regime (Ch 2).
observed: Input-heavy alone does not establish memory-capacity-bound or prefill-dominated. Capacity depends on concurrency, KV precision, context length, weights, batching, and hardware. Prefill may dominate FLOPs while decode dominates wall-clock.
evidence: The canonical example itself shows prefill at ~13% of wall-clock while dominating token/FLOP count; capacity depends on the 436 GB KV budget and concurrency.
root_cause: Universal claim derived from one workload profile.
correction: Qualify as a first-order tendency for the canonical workload. Distinguish token/FLOP mix from memory-capacity pressure and wall-clock dominance.
acceptance_test: The text does not infer memory-capacity-bound or prefill-dominated status from input-heavy alone.

quoted_clause: If the workload were output-heavy, it would be decode-bandwidth-bound.
observed: Output-heavy workloads can be compute-bound at high batch, latency-bound at low batch, or bandwidth-bound depending on model, hardware, and serving configuration. Output-heavy alone does not determine the bottleneck.
evidence: The book elsewhere treats compute-bound versus bandwidth-bound as regime-dependent on batch, sequence length, precision, kernels, and hardware.
root_cause: Overgeneralization from a first-order regime to a universal consequence.
correction: Say output-heavy shifts the token/FLOP mix toward decode and often makes decode bandwidth/latency critical, but the actual bottleneck must be measured.
acceptance_test: The text presents decode-bandwidth-bound as a possible regime, not a necessary consequence of output-heavy workload.

page_hint: Ch 5 §3(a), takeaway for canonical RAG workload
quoted_clause: It places the workload in the quality-positive regime
observed: 'Quality-positive regime' is undefined and unsupported. No evidence is given that all-mpnet-base-v2 is quality-positive for this corpus or that the 384-dim option is not.
evidence: The preceding text says dimension alone is not a cross-model quality metric and that quality must be validated on the target corpus.
root_cause: Vague, unsupported quality claim.
correction: Define 'quality-positive regime' or replace it with a scoped statement such as 'expected to meet the retrieval-quality target under the stated assumptions; validate on the target corpus'.
acceptance_test: The term is defined or removed, and the quality claim is scoped to evidence or assumption.

quoted_clause: Fine-tuning becomes compelling only when the query distribution is highly concentrated, the domain vocabulary is extremely specialized, and the workload volume sustains the training amortization threshold.
observed: 'Only when' overstates the case. Fine-tuning for style, format, tool-use policy, or behavior shaping can be compelling under other conditions, as the section itself acknowledges.
evidence: Earlier text says fine-tuning shapes behavior, style, task patterns, format, and tool-use policy, not only specialized vocabulary or concentrated queries.
root_cause: Universal claim inconsistent with the section's own mechanism discussion.
correction: Soften to 'most compelling when...' and acknowledge style/format/tool-policy cases.
acceptance_test: The sentence no longer uses 'only when' unless the exclusivity is defended.

quoted_clause: The real cost changes are: (a) one-time training compute, and (b) incremental storage, both against the RAG pipeline's prefill cost (~1.08 s, which dominates any plausible TTFT delta).
observed: This mixes monetary cost with latency. Prefill time is not a monetary cost, and fine-tuning does not necessarily change prefill time. The comparison should separate cost accounting from latency accounting.
evidence: The sentence lists cost changes but then compares them to a latency figure (~1.08 s).
root_cause: Category error: cost versus latency.
correction: Separate the monetary comparison (training + storage cost) from the latency comparison (TTFT effect must be measured). Do not call prefill time a cost.
acceptance_test: Cost and latency claims are in separate sentences with correct units.

quoted_clause: the top-of-range ~15% MAP gain (reports span a few to ~15%, domain- and corpus-specific — §3)
observed: The ~15% figure is a general dimension-quality range, not a measured gain for all-mpnet-base-v2 versus MiniLM or for the canonical corpus. Using it as the expected gain for this model pair is unsupported.
evidence: The text itself says the range is domain- and corpus-specific and that dimension alone is not a cross-model quality metric.
root_cause: Unsupported linkage between a general reported range and a specific model comparison.
correction: Label the 15% as an illustrative upper bound from the literature, not an expected gain for this pair; require target-corpus measurement.
acceptance_test: The 15% figure is not used as a decision input without an explicit assumption label and target-corpus validation requirement.

quoted_clause: the value scales linearly with query length, so the model-to-model ratio equals the parameter ratio (bge-large ≈ 3× mpnet)
observed: The ratio equals the parameter ratio only under the same architecture and ignoring attention/non-parameter operations. These are different architectures (MiniLM, mpnet, bge), so the approximation is not generally exact.
evidence: The formula 2×params×L is a parameter-count approximation; attention and other operations vary by architecture.
root_cause: Overgeneralization of a simplified FLOP formula.
correction: Say the ratio is approximately the parameter ratio under the same architecture and sequence length; for cross-architecture comparisons, treat it as an estimate.
acceptance_test: The text qualifies the parameter-ratio claim as an approximation and architecture-dependent.

quoted_clause: modal branches
observed: Likely intended 'modality branches'. 'Modal branches' is ambiguous and may confuse readers.
evidence: The surrounding sentence discusses vision encoders, projectors, and tool-use workloads, i.e. modalities.
root_cause: Typo/terminology slip.
correction: Change 'modal branches' to 'modality branches'.
acceptance_test: The phrase reads 'modality branches'.

page_hint: Ch 5 §3(a), takeaway for canonical RAG workload
quoted_clause: before paying it..
observed: Double period.
evidence: Punctuation artifact at the end of the sentence.
root_cause: Typo.
correction: Replace 'it..' with 'it.'
acceptance_test: Single terminal period.

quoted_clause: KV cache per-token figures are at FP16 (~2.62 MB/token) unless an 8-bit (~1.31 MB/token) variant is explicitly stated.
observed: This KV-cache reminder is placed in the embedding-model selection subsection. Embedding encoders for retrieval do not use the autoregressive KV cache being described; the note belongs in the generation-model subsection.
evidence: The surrounding paragraph discusses embedding dimension, parameter count, and retrieval quality, not generation KV residency.
root_cause: Misplaced cross-section reminder.
correction: Move the KV-cache precision note to the generation-model subsection or remove it from the embedding subsection.
acceptance_test: The KV-cache note appears only where generation KV residency is discussed.

page_hint: Ch 6, 'Reading Telemetry Into a Decision' and §8 mini-case; cross-check Ch 7 Table 7-1 note
quoted_clause: aggregate prefill demand at the 40 rps peak is 40 × 1.29 ≈ 52 PFLOP/s vs the 8×H100 aggregate ~7.9 PFLOPS, ~6.5× oversubscribed
observed: The 40 rps peak is the canonical fleet-level workload, but the comparison uses one 8×H100 host's aggregate peak. If 40 rps is per host, the same example is impossible under the stated KV budget: 40 rps × ~8.6 s service ≈ 344 concurrent requests, versus ~17.5 requests/host. The mini-case's 85% KV occupancy and 'architecture is memory- and compute-sane at the 10 rps design point' cannot both be true under the same denominator.
evidence: Ch 7 states the canonical scenario is ~10 rps average / ~40 rps peak served by a 70B FP16 model on an 8×H100 host, and Table 7-1's note gives ~436 GB KV budget and ~17.5 requests/host. The chunk also gives 1.08 s prefill + 300 output tokens × ~25 ms TPOT ≈ 8.6 s service. 40 × 8.6 ≈ 344 concurrent; 344 / 17.5 ≈ 19.7 hosts. If 40 rps is fleet-level, the correct prefill comparison is against fleet aggregate (~21 × 7.9 ≈ 166 PFLOPS), not one host's 7.9 PFLOPS. If 40 rps is per host, the KV concurrency is impossible. Either reading breaks the example.
root_cause: Denominator/population mixing: fleet-level rps is compared to single-host compute capacity, while the KV occupancy and 'sane at 10 rps' claims implicitly use a different host count.
correction: State the host count explicitly in the telemetry trace and mini-case. If 40 rps is fleet-level, compare 52 PFLOP/s to the fleet aggregate and show per-host prefill/queue behavior. If 40 rps is per host, recompute the required host count and KV concurrency, and do not claim 85% KV occupancy at that load. Re-derive the '10 rps design point' with the same host count.
acceptance_test: A reader can reproduce the same host count from the rps, service time, KV budget, and aggregate PFLOPS, and the 85% KV occupancy, 6.5× oversubscription, and 'sane at 10 rps' statements all agree under one explicit denominator.

quoted_clause: the prefill pass for 9,200 input tokens costs ≈ 2 × 70e9 params × 9.2e3 tokens ≈ 1.29 PFLOP of linear (2PL) FLOPs (the quadratic attention term adds ≈ 0.2 PFLOP at 9.2K — ≈ 1.5 PFLOP full-square total), which against the ~1.08 s prefill budget implies a required rate of ≈ 1.19 PFLOPS
observed: The prose acknowledges a ~1.5 PFLOP full-square total but then divides only the 1.29 PFLOP linear term by 1.08 s. The full-square required rate is ~1.5 / 1.08 ≈ 1.39 PFLOPS, not 1.19. Table 6-1 and the caption repeat the 1.19 figure and the ~9,200 FLOP/byte intensity, which are linear-only values.
evidence: 1.29 PFLOP / 1.08 s = 1.194 PFLOPS. 1.5 PFLOP / 1.08 s = 1.389 PFLOPS. The attention term is ~0.2 PFLOP, so the full-square intensity is ~1.5e15 / 140e9 ≈ 10,700 FLOP/byte, not ~9,200. The conclusion that prefill exceeds one H100 still holds, but the printed rate and intensity are inconsistent with the stated full-square total.
root_cause: Mixing linear-only and full-square FLOP bases within one calculation and then propagating the linear-only result into the table and caption.
correction: Either use the linear-only 1.29 PFLOP consistently and remove the full-square total from the same calculation, or use the full-square ~1.5 PFLOP and print ~1.39 PFLOPS and ~10.7K FLOP/byte. State which basis Table 6-1 uses.
acceptance_test: Every prefill rate, intensity, and table entry in Ch 6 uses one explicitly named FLOP basis, and the arithmetic from that basis to the printed number is reproducible.

page_hint: Ch 6, 'Reading Telemetry Into a Decision' and §8 mini-case
quoted_clause: low prefix-cache hit means many independent 9.2K prefixes are being prefill-processed from scratch ... enable prefix / RadixAttention-style caching ... so shared retrieved-context prefixes are reused
observed: The diagnosis says the prefixes are 'independent,' but the remedy assumes they are 'shared.' If the prefixes are genuinely independent, prefix caching cannot collapse them. If they are shared but the cache is disabled or missing, the text should say that. The mini-case repeats 'repeated full 9.2K prefills (low prefix hit)' without distinguishing unique prefixes from cache-disabled shared prefixes.
evidence: Prefix caching saves prefill work only when multiple requests share a common prefix. A low hit ratio can mean either (a) the cache is not enabled, (b) the cache is enabled but the workload has low prefix sharing, or (c) the cache policy is evicting useful blocks. The recommended fix is valid only for (a) or (c), not for (b).
root_cause: The trace does not separate cache-disabled from low-sharing workload; 'independent' and 'shared' are used as if interchangeable.
correction: Add the missing discriminator: report prefix-sharing distribution or cache-enabled status. If prefixes are unique, the remedy is not prefix caching; it is capacity, admission control, or workload reshaping. If prefixes are shared but the cache is off, say so explicitly.
acceptance_test: The telemetry trace states whether the low hit ratio is caused by cache-disabled shared prefixes or by genuinely unique prefixes, and the recommended fix follows from that distinction.

quoted_clause: Bandwidth-bound decode + compute-bound prefill ⇒ P/D disaggregation ... is the remedy at scale, because squeezing both regimes from one resource pool fights itself.
observed: The implication arrow presents P/D disaggregation as the remedy without stating the conditions under which it helps or the costs it introduces. P/D disaggregation adds KV transfer, separate pools, scheduling complexity, and possible idle capacity; it is not universally superior to a well-scheduled colocated pool.
evidence: The same section elsewhere qualifies other optimizations (prefix caching, KV quantization, speculative decoding) with scope warnings. P/D disaggregation receives no equivalent trade-off treatment in this chunk.
root_cause: Architecture recommendation stated as a direct consequence of regime difference without alternatives or boundary conditions.
correction: Reframe as a candidate remedy: state the conditions (e.g., long prefill/decode imbalance, sufficient scale, KV-transfer cost below interference savings, workload mix that benefits from separate pools) and the costs (KV migration, added failure domains, pool sizing). Compare with colocated scheduling and chunked prefill.
acceptance_test: A reader can explain when P/D disaggregation is likely to help, when it is likely to hurt, and what telemetry would justify it over a colocated alternative.

quoted_clause: the ~436 GB KV budget and ~17.5 requests/host (byte-accurate 17.51; conservative integer floor 17)
observed: The 17.5 requests/host figure is derived from the 9.5K max KV per request and the 436 GB budget. It is correct as a single-request concurrency bound, but the surrounding text sometimes uses it as if it were a throughput or load capacity. At 8.6 s service, 17.5 concurrent requests imply only ~2.0 rps per host, not 10 rps or 40 rps.
evidence: 436 GB / 24.9 GB ≈ 17.5. 17.5 / 8.6 s ≈ 2.03 rps per host. The canonical 10 rps average / 40 rps peak therefore requires ~5 hosts at average and ~20 hosts at peak, not one host. This is consistent with a fleet-level reading but conflicts with any sentence that treats 40 rps as a single-host load.
root_cause: Concurrency capacity (requests resident) is being conflated with request rate (requests per second) without dividing by service time.
correction: Add the missing conversion explicitly: max sustainable rps per host ≈ (KV-limited concurrency) / (service time). Use that to derive host count for 10 rps and 40 rps. Keep '17.5 requests/host' labeled as a concurrency bound, not a throughput figure.
acceptance_test: Every use of 17.5 requests/host is accompanied by the service-time conversion when used to reason about rps, and the host count for 10 rps and 40 rps is reproducible.

quoted_clause: = 2,560 KiB = 2.5 MiB; exact decimal 2.62 MB
observed: 2,621,440 bytes is exactly 2.62144 MB in decimal, not 2.62 MB. The row uses '≈' in the value column but then says 'exact decimal 2.62 MB.'
evidence: 2 × 80 × 8192 × 2 = 2,621,440 bytes = 2.62144 MB = 2.5 MiB. The printed 2.62 MB is a rounded value.
root_cause: Rounding label applied to an already rounded decimal.
correction: Change 'exact decimal 2.62 MB' to '≈2.62 MB (2.62144 MB exact)' or simply '2.62144 MB exact; ≈2.62 MB displayed.'
acceptance_test: The table does not call a rounded decimal 'exact' while also printing the unrounded byte count.

quoted_clause: We keep the full-MHA bound as the canonical conservative residual because an architect should size against the worst case the chosen model actually presents
observed: If the chosen model uses GQA, the full-MHA geometry is not the worst case that model presents; it is a different, more conservative geometry. The sentence conflates 'conservative teaching bound' with 'worst case of the chosen model.'
evidence: The same paragraph correctly says the honest move is to read the model card's KV-head count and substitute it into the GQA formula. That is the actual worst case for the chosen model.
root_cause: Two different purposes—canonical teaching geometry and per-model sizing—are compressed into one sentence.
correction: Say: 'We keep full-MHA as the canonical teaching bound. For a real model, use its actual KV-head count; do not treat full-MHA as that model's worst case unless the model is full-MHA.'
acceptance_test: The text distinguishes the canonical teaching geometry from the chosen model's actual worst-case KV geometry.

quoted_clause: If it does not fit, every subsequent decision (offload, recompute, page) is a degradation, not a cost-optimization.
observed: Offload, recompute, and paging can be deliberate cost-optimizations when the SLO permits slower memory tiers. The absolute 'every ... is a degradation, not a cost-optimization' overstates the case.
evidence: The chapter itself later treats CPU offload as a mechanism that 'can reduce GPU residency while adding host-memory and transfer requirements,' which is a trade-off, not purely a degradation.
root_cause: Rhetorical absolute applied to a trade-off space.
correction: Soften to: 'If the residency floor does not fit, offload, recompute, or paging become necessary trade-offs; they may be acceptable cost optimizations only when the added latency/transfer cost stays within the SLO.'
acceptance_test: The text does not classify all offload/recompute/paging as degradations while later presenting them as legitimate trade-offs.

quoted_clause: The per-token KV footprint of a fully-cached (MHA) attention head is $$ KV_{\text{per-token}} = 2 \times n_\text{layers} \times d_\text{hidden} \times \text{bytes-per-value} $$
observed: The formula computes the whole-model KV footprint across all heads, but the prose calls it the footprint of an 'attention head.' For one head, the width should be d_head, not d_hidden.
evidence: For the canonical 70B MHA example, 2 × 80 × 8192 × 2 B = 2,621,440 B/token is the whole-model value. A single head with d_head = 128 would be 2 × 80 × 128 × 2 B = 40,960 B/token. The parenthetical '(one key and one value per layer, each d_hidden wide)' also describes the concatenated K/V across heads, not one head.
root_cause: Terminology drift between 'attention head' and 'model-level KV width' in the definition of the canonical formula.
correction: Change to 'The per-token KV footprint of a fully-cached MHA model is ...' and clarify that d_hidden is the total K/V width across all heads; if discussing a single head, use d_head and multiply by n_heads.
acceptance_test: The prose, formula, and worked 70B example all agree that the formula is model-level; a reader cannot infer that one head has width d_hidden.

page_hint: Ch. 7 §6 Architecture Consequence, KV quantization bullet
quoted_clause: This is a *memory* lever, orthogonal to bandwidth/compute fixes — the architect pulls it when the KV floor, not decode bandwidth, binds.
observed: KV quantization is described as orthogonal to bandwidth, but reducing KV precision also reduces the bytes of K/V state read during decode, which can directly relieve KV-bandwidth pressure. It is not compute-reducing, but it is not bandwidth-orthogonal.
evidence: Decode reads historical K/V tensors from HBM each token. Halving KV bytes per element reduces KV read traffic, subject to layout, metadata, and kernel behavior. The same section elsewhere correctly says FP8 KV halves raw tensor bytes; that byte reduction is exactly what can affect bandwidth-bound decode.
root_cause: Conflating 'primarily a capacity lever' with 'orthogonal to bandwidth.'
correction: Rewrite as: 'KV quantization is primarily a capacity lever; it can also reduce KV read bandwidth during decode, but it does not reduce attention FLOPs. Pull it when KV capacity binds, and benchmark it when decode bandwidth may also be limiting.'
acceptance_test: The text no longer claims KV quantization is orthogonal to bandwidth, and it distinguishes capacity, bandwidth, and compute effects.

quoted_clause: The memory floor is the first constraint every architecture decision respects, because unlike compute or bandwidth it cannot be moved by better kernels — it is fixed by weights + KV + (for training) optimizer state.
observed: The claim that the memory floor 'cannot be moved by better kernels' and is 'fixed by weights + KV' is too strong. The chapter itself discusses weight quantization, KV quantization, mixed precision, offloading, and runtime layout choices that change the memory floor. Better kernels can also reduce workspace or enable more memory-efficient layouts.
evidence: Earlier in the same chapter, MXFP4/BF16 mixed precision reduces 70B weight storage from 140 GB to 39.24375 GB, and FP8 KV reduces KV from ~2.62 MB/token to ~1.31 MB/token. Those are representation choices, not merely kernels, but they directly move the floor. The sentence's absolute wording contradicts the chapter's own mechanisms.
root_cause: Rhetorical overstatement of a useful first-order point: raw tensor residency is not reduced by faster arithmetic alone.
correction: Rewrite as: 'The memory floor is a first-order constraint because faster kernels alone do not reduce the bytes that must reside; it is set by representation and residency choices — weights, KV, optimizer state, workspace, and runtime layout.'
acceptance_test: The text no longer says the floor is fixed or cannot be moved, and it explicitly acknowledges quantization/offloading/layout as ways the floor changes.

page_hint: Ch. 7 §5 Common Mistakes, fourth bullet; also §4 item 4
quoted_clause: FP8 KV ≈50% of FP16 (raw byte-halving) is what serving stacks realize today
observed: This is an overgeneralized empirical claim about 'serving stacks' and conflicts with the same section's later warning: 'Do not generalize a fixed ratio to all FP8-KV deployments.' The raw payload ratio is 50%, but realized memory and bandwidth effects vary by engine, layout, metadata, allocator rounding, and accounting boundary.
evidence: The text itself says the realized per-token footprint depends on engine version, cache-block layout, scale/offset metadata, allocator rounding, and accounting boundary. Therefore 'what serving stacks realize today' cannot be stated as a universal 50%.
root_cause: Mixing a nominal raw-payload ratio with a realized deployment claim.
correction: Say: 'FP8 KV has a nominal 50% raw-payload ratio versus FP16; realized savings vary by serving stack and must be re-derived.' Remove 'is what serving stacks realize today' or scope it to a named, dated measurement.
acceptance_test: No unqualified claim that serving stacks realize 50%; the nominal ratio and realized ratio are clearly separated.

quoted_clause: 128K context drives KV to ~335 GB, which forces quantization or model parallelism.
observed: On the canonical 8×H100 host with 640 GB aggregate HBM, 335 GB of KV plus 140 GB of FP16 weights is ~475 GB, which fits within 640 GB. The statement is only true relative to a smaller device or a different host configuration; it is not a universal consequence.
evidence: 140 GB weights + 335.5 GB KV = 475.5 GB, below 640 GB. The chapter's own canonical host is 8×H100. Therefore 128K context does not by itself force quantization or additional model parallelism on that host, though it may force a larger topology than a 2×H100 configuration.
root_cause: Missing scope: the claim implicitly assumes a single GPU or a smaller aggregate pool.
correction: Rewrite as: 'On a single 80 GB GPU, 128K context forces quantization, offloading, or model parallelism; on the canonical 8×H100 host, ~475 GB total residency fits in 640 GB but leaves less headroom for concurrency and workspace.'
acceptance_test: The claim is explicitly scoped to a device or host configuration and does not imply that 128K always forces quantization or model parallelism.

quoted_clause: (The vLLM "54%" figure is a decode inter-token-latency slope ratio, not a memory ratio.)
observed: A specific vLLM figure is asserted without a citation in this chunk. It is also time-sensitive and implementation-specific.
evidence: The surrounding paragraph otherwise cites primary sources for AWQ, GPTQ, GGUF, MXFP4, NVFP4, OFP8, SmoothQuant, QLoRA, and KIVI. This vLLM claim has no adjacent source or date.
root_cause: Specific empirical claim introduced without provenance.
correction: Add a dated citation to the vLLM measurement or remove the parenthetical. If retained, state the exact workload, metric, and version.
acceptance_test: The vLLM 54% claim has a source and scope, or is removed.

quoted_clause: realized savings land between, once block/scale metadata is counted
observed: The phrase 'land between' is ambiguous because the preceding quantities mix a percentage reduction (50%) with a multiplicative bound (4×). It is unclear whether realized savings are between 2× and 4×, between 50% and 75%, or something else.
evidence: FP8 KV is described as ≈50% of FP16 (a 2× reduction), while 4-bit KV is described as a full 4× reduction. 'Between' those two requires a consistent unit.
root_cause: Unit mismatch in a comparative claim.
correction: Rewrite in one unit, e.g. 'realized reduction is typically between the FP8 nominal 2× and the 4-bit raw bound of 4×, depending on metadata and layout.'
acceptance_test: The comparison uses one consistent unit and a reader can state the lower and upper bounds without guessing.

page_hint: Ch 7, Fig 7.7/7.8 and end-of-chapter mini-case (PDF page not available in chunk)
quoted_clause: ≈165 GB ... nominal 160 GB aggregate HBM of 2×80 GB H100s
observed: The manuscript mixes decimal GB for weights/KV (140 GB = 70B×2 bytes; 24.9 GB = 9.5K×2.62 MB) with nominal H100 '80 GB' capacity. If 80 GB is 80 GiB (81,920 MiB), 2×80 GiB = 171.8 GB decimal, so 165 GB fits nominal capacity; if 80 GB is decimal, 160 GB, it does not. The same ambiguity affects '640 GB' and '436 GB' in Fig 7.7/7.8.
root_cause: Unit convention not fixed for GPU capacity vs decimal byte arithmetic.
correction: State whether H100 80 GB is treated as 80×10^9 B or 80 GiB; convert all canonical memory arithmetic to one unit; include runtime reserve in the 2×H100 fit test; recompute 436 GB and 17.5 concurrency.
acceptance_test: A byte-level ledger shows weights, KV, runtime, and HBM capacity in the same unit; 2×H100 fit conclusion and 436/24.9 concurrency reproduce under the stated convention.

quoted_clause: FLOPs scale linearly with parameter count and context length
observed: Attention FLOPs scale quadratically with context length; the same section later says 'attention work grows quadratically with L.' The sentence is false as written.
evidence: Standard transformer prefill: projection FLOPs ~2N per token (linear in tokens), attention score/value FLOPs ~O(L^2 d) per layer; total is not linear in context length. The manuscript's own later statement contradicts it.
root_cause: Overgeneralization from projection-dominated arithmetic.
correction: Say: 'FLOPs scale linearly with parameter count and token count for projection-dominated work; attention adds a term quadratic in context length.'
acceptance_test: The sentence and later quadratic statement are consistent; a worked L=9.2K vs 32K example shows the attention term.

page_hint: Ch 7, What We Still Don't Know, third bullet
quoted_clause: Whether per-request KV caching can be partially offloaded to CPU DRAM during decode without TTFT impact, beyond the vLLM KV Offloading Connector's 2–22× TTFT reduction range [S7][1P][FACT]
observed: The bullet conflates two mechanisms: (a) offloading KV during decode, which affects decode latency/TPOT/ITL and capacity, not TTFT (TTFT is already past); and (b) prefix/KV reuse from CPU, which can reduce TTFT for repeated prefixes. The cited 2–22× TTFT reduction cannot be attributed to decode-time offload without an event trace.
evidence: TTFT is measured from request arrival to first output token, before autoregressive decode. Offloading KV during decode cannot change that interval. A TTFT reduction from a KV offloading connector is plausibly a prefix-cache hit path, not decode offload.
root_cause: Mechanism/metric conflation.
correction: Split into two claims: decode-time KV offload trades TPOT/ITL and capacity; prefix/KV reuse from CPU can reduce TTFT for cache-hit requests. State the vLLM connector's measured metric and cache-hit conditions.
acceptance_test: An event trace with prefill, first token, decode, and cache hit shows which interval changes; the text attributes the 2–22× range to the correct mechanism.

page_hint: Ch 8, 'Three different bounds' block and roadmap
quoted_clause: prefill is compute-bound (high intensity), decode is bandwidth-bound (low intensity)
observed: Presented as a property of the canonical RAG workload 'without overlap,' but the regime depends on model architecture, sequence length, batch/concurrency, precision, kernels, hardware, and serving configuration. In continuous batching/chunked prefill, prefill and decode can overlap across requests.
evidence: Roofline position is workload- and implementation-dependent; large-batch decode can become compute-bound; very short prefill can be launch/bandwidth-bound; chunked prefill mixes phases.
root_cause: First-order regime stated as universal law.
correction: Scope: 'At the canonical 9.2K prefill and low-batch decode, prefill is typically compute-bound and decode bandwidth-bound; both shift with batching, context, precision, and kernels. In a serving system they can overlap across requests.'
acceptance_test: The text names at least one condition under which each regime flips and cross-references continuous batching/chunked prefill.

quoted_clause: only ~1–2 at 128K
observed: For FP16 KV at 128K, 436 GB / 335 GB ≈ 1.30, so the integer concurrency floor is 1, not 1–2. The '2' only appears if FP8 KV is included (436/167.5 ≈ 2.6, floor 2). The caption says 'FP16 KV cache (orange)'.
root_cause: Mixing FP16 and FP8 cases in one range without labeling.
correction: State '~1.3 (floor 1) at 128K FP16; ~2.6 (floor 2) at 128K FP8' or label the range as spanning both precisions.
acceptance_test: The caption's integer concurrency matches the stated precision and the 436 GB budget.

quoted_clause: the ~64 GB runtime/NCCL reserve is per-host (not per-rank)
observed: NCCL buffers and CUDA contexts are per-process/GPU (per rank), not per-host. A 64 GB host-level reserve may be an aggregate budget, but its components are allocated per rank. The phrase can mislead per-rank fit arithmetic.
evidence: NCCL allocates communication buffers per rank/GPU; CUDA context and workspace are per device. A host-level total can be divided across ranks, but it is not a single per-host allocation.
root_cause: Modeling aggregate reserve as a per-host resource.
correction: Say: 'The ~64 GB is an aggregate host reserve allocated across the eight ranks (~8 GB/rank); NCCL buffers and CUDA contexts are per-rank.'
acceptance_test: The per-rank fit calculation shows the reserve allocated per rank and sums to the host total.

quoted_clause: The next step — turning '5,000 employees' into ~2,000 registered users ... is Chapter 4's job (workload anatomy).
observed: The mini-case is at the end of Ch 7, after Ch 4. Calling Ch 4 the 'next step' is a backward reference that breaks the reader's progression; the mini-case also says 'From the unit-and-token work of Ch 1 alone' before using Ch 7 KV arithmetic.
evidence: Chapter order: Ch 1 tokens, Ch 4 workload anatomy, Ch 7 memory. A reader at Ch 7 has already completed Ch 4.
root_cause: Mini-case written as if it were placed before Ch 4, or not updated after restructuring.
correction: Reframe as 'Chapter 4's workload-anatomy method (already developed) would turn...' or move the mini-case to the end of Ch 4. Remove 'from Ch 1 alone' or say 'using Ch 1's token units and Ch 7's KV arithmetic.'
acceptance_test: The mini-case's forward/backward references match the final chapter order.

quoted_clause: the workload is input-heavy (retrieved context dominates)
observed: This is asserted as a fact established 'from the unit-and-token work of Ch 1 alone.' Ch 1 establishes token units, not the retrieval workload's input/output ratio. The ratio depends on retrieval depth, chunk size, prompt template, and output length.
evidence: A wiki Q&A system could use short retrieved snippets and long answers, or long multi-document context and short answers. The initial ask does not determine it.
root_cause: Scenario assumption presented as derived fact.
correction: Label it [ASSUMPTION] and say it must be validated in Ch 4 workload characterization; show how the memory conclusion changes if output-heavy.
acceptance_test: The mini-case distinguishes derived token arithmetic from workload assumptions and includes a sensitivity check.

quoted_clause: The hierarchy runs from the smallest/fastest/closest resource (registers, tensor cores, on-chip SRAM) to the largest/slower/farther (HBM, GPU interconnect, other GPUs).
observed: Tensor cores are execution resources, not a memory/storage level; GPU interconnect and other GPUs are communication topology, not a memory level. The caption conflates compute, memory, and interconnect into one 'hierarchy,' then says each is 'a different level of this ladder.'
evidence: A memory hierarchy is registers → shared memory/L1 → L2 → HBM; compute units (SMs, tensor cores) execute on data; interconnect moves data between devices. They are distinct resource classes.
root_cause: Category error in the ladder metaphor.
correction: Separate the figure into (a) execution resources, (b) memory hierarchy, (c) interconnect topology; or rename it 'resource stack' and explicitly distinguish compute, storage, and communication.
acceptance_test: The figure/caption visually distinguishes compute units from storage levels and from interconnect; no resource is called a 'level' of the wrong hierarchy.

quoted_clause: the roofline's vertical axis (peak TFLOPS) and horizontal axis (FLOP/byte) are both determined by *where* on this hierarchy the work sits.
observed: The vertical axis is the hardware's attainable performance ceiling (peak TFLOPS/bandwidth), not determined by where the work sits; the horizontal axis is the kernel's arithmetic intensity, determined by algorithm, data reuse, and access pattern. The kernel's position depends on both hardware and implementation.
evidence: Standard roofline: vertical = performance (FLOP/s), horizontal = arithmetic intensity (FLOP/byte); the roof is set by hardware peaks, the kernel's x-position by its data movement per FLOP.
root_cause: Conflating hardware ceiling with kernel position.
correction: Say: 'The roofline's ceiling is set by the hardware hierarchy; a kernel's horizontal position is set by its arithmetic intensity. The kernel's regime is where its intensity meets that ceiling.'
acceptance_test: The text correctly distinguishes hardware peak, kernel intensity, and ridge point.

page_hint: Ch 7, What We Still Don't Know, fourth bullet
quoted_clause: All four 2026-class open architectures attack KV cache size at the attention layer itself
observed: The four cited descriptions do not all establish KV-cache-size reduction. Kimi K3 is described as targeting 'information flow across long sequences'; Qwen3.8-Flash-Next as addressing 'long-context cost.' Those may be compute or quality changes, not KV bytes/token. The DeepSeek percentages also lack a stated baseline/model-size comparability.
evidence: A KV-size claim requires a bytes/token or context-per-byte metric under a stated baseline. 'Information flow' and 'long-context cost' are not that metric.
root_cause: Overgeneralizing from a set of related long-context architectures to a single KV-size claim.
correction: Separate (a) measured KV-size reductions (DeepSeek, GLM if baseline stated) from (b) long-context information-flow/compute changes (Kimi, Qwen). State baseline, model size, context, and metric for each percentage.
acceptance_test: Each cited model's claim maps to a KV bytes/token or context-per-byte number under a stated baseline, or is explicitly labeled as a non-KV long-context change.

page_hint: Ch 7, What We Still Don't Know, fifth bullet
quoted_clause: The total-vs-active and MoE-vs-dense facts of Ch 3 ... confirm that attention layers process every token densely and emit key/value per token
observed: The conclusion is correct for standard MoE, but it does not follow from total-vs-active parameter facts alone. Those facts establish that MoE routing sparsifies the MLP experts; they do not establish that attention is dense. A sparse-attention or hybrid-attention MoE would violate the inference.
evidence: MoE routing applies to expert MLP layers; attention geometry is a separate architectural choice. The text itself later says hybrid-attention models change KV.
root_cause: Non sequitur from parameter-count facts to attention density.
correction: State the architectural assumption: 'In the standard MoE architectures considered here, routing selects MLP experts; attention remains dense, so KV is emitted per token. This must be checked per model, especially for hybrid-attention MoE.'
acceptance_test: The text cites the model's attention architecture, not just total-vs-active parameter counts, before concluding MoE sparsity does not reduce KV.

quoted_clause: Memory-capacity-constrained (equivalently KV-capacity-constrained)
observed: Memory capacity can be consumed by weights, activations, workspace, and KV; equating capacity constraint with KV capacity is too narrow. In the canonical long-context case KV dominates, but not universally.
evidence: A model with large weights or large activation workspace can be capacity-constrained even with short KV; a small model with long context can be KV-capacity-constrained.
root_cause: Canonical-case shorthand presented as definition.
correction: Say: 'Memory-capacity-constrained (often KV-capacity-constrained in long-context inference) means...' and name the dominant resident component.
acceptance_test: The definition allows non-KV capacity constraints and the canonical case is labeled as such.

quoted_clause: every attention weight update
observed: Inference computes attention scores/weights; it does not update attention weights. 'Weight update' is training terminology and can mislead.
evidence: Autoregressive inference has no gradient update; attention weights are computed from QK^T and softmax.
root_cause: Terminology drift from training.
correction: Say 'every attention-score computation' or 'every attention-weight computation.'
acceptance_test: Search shows no 'weight update' in inference compute context.

quoted_clause: In FP16, a single multiply-add counts as two FLOPs.
observed: A multiply-add counts as two FLOPs regardless of precision; FP16 affects throughput and rounding, not the FLOP count convention. The sentence implies precision changes the count.
evidence: FLOP counting convention: one FMA = 2 FLOPs (one multiply + one add). Precision changes operations/second, not FLOPs/operation.
root_cause: Conflating FLOP count with precision throughput.
correction: Say: 'A single multiply-add counts as two FLOPs; FP16 affects throughput, not the count.'
acceptance_test: The text separates FLOP count from precision-dependent throughput.

quoted_clause: whether increasing FLOPs will actually reduce latency
observed: Increasing FLOPs adds work; it cannot by itself reduce latency. The intended meaning is increasing compute throughput or adding compute resources.
evidence: Latency = work / throughput; adding work increases numerator. Roofline tells whether adding compute resources helps or whether memory bandwidth is the limit.
root_cause: Sloppy causal wording.
correction: Say: 'whether adding compute throughput/resources will reduce latency, or whether the kernel is already starved for bytes.'
acceptance_test: The sentence's causal direction is correct.

quoted_clause: The trip time is determined by the ridge point and 'peak TFLOPS on the vertical axis'
observed: The ridge point determines the regime, not the trip time; trip time is max(compute time, memory time) plus other costs. The roofline vertical axis is attainable performance, with peak TFLOPS as the ceiling, not the axis itself.
evidence: Roofline: y = min(peak compute, intensity × bandwidth); ridge is where the two terms meet. The y-axis is performance, not 'peak TFLOPS.'
root_cause: Imprecise mental-model shorthand.
correction: Say: 'The ridge point tells us which ceiling binds; trip time is set by the binding ceiling and other overheads. The roofline's vertical axis is attainable performance, capped by peak TFLOPS.'
acceptance_test: The mental model correctly distinguishes ridge, ceiling, and latency.

page_hint: Ch 7, What We Still Don't Know, second bullet
quoted_clause: at very long context lengths (128K+, MoE experts)
observed: 'MoE experts' is a model architecture, not a context length. The parenthetical conflates two dimensions.
evidence: Context length is measured in tokens; MoE is a model architecture. The sentence should say 'at very long context lengths (128K+) and in MoE models.'
root_cause: Compressed list conflating categories.
correction: Say: 'at very long context lengths (128K+) and in MoE models.'
acceptance_test: The sentence separates context length from model architecture.

quoted_clause: §4 turns to measurement, §5 to common mistakes, §6 to architecture consequences, and §8 closes with a mini-case
observed: The roadmap skips §7 (presumably 'What We Still Don't Know') and says §1–§3 build arithmetic though §2 is Mental Model. This is a navigation inconsistency.
evidence: The chapter's own section numbering includes §7; the roadmap should account for it.
root_cause: Stale roadmap after section insertion.
correction: Add §7 and describe §2 accurately.
acceptance_test: The roadmap matches the actual section list.

page_hint: Ch 7, What We Still Don't Know, second bullet
quoted_clause: The primary sources anchor FP8 KV ≈50% of FP16 (raw byte-halving) at near-zero quality loss
observed: 'Near-zero quality loss' is a strong empirical claim without an inline citation or scope (model, benchmark, context length). The bullet says 'primary sources' but does not name them.
evidence: FP8 KV quality loss is workload- and implementation-dependent; 'near-zero' needs a benchmark and context.
root_cause: Claim strength exceeds cited evidence.
correction: Add citation and scope, or soften to 'small quality loss in the cited benchmarks.'
acceptance_test: The claim names source, model, benchmark, and context length.

quoted_clause: query-key, value-aggregation, and MLP projections
observed: Query-key and value-aggregation are attention matmuls, not projections; only the MLP projections are projections. The list conflates operation types.
evidence: QK^T computes attention scores; attention-weight × V aggregates values; MLP projections are linear layers.
root_cause: Imprecise operation naming.
correction: Say 'QK^T, attention-value aggregation, and MLP matmuls' or separate projections from attention matmuls.
acceptance_test: The operation names match the transformer computation.

quoted_clause: A kernel is compute-bound when its FLOPs run on the tensor cores and data fits in on-chip memory (high arithmetic intensity)
observed: Compute-bound is defined by arithmetic intensity above the ridge point, not by data fitting on-chip. Data can fit on-chip yet still be memory-bound if reuse is low; data can stream from HBM yet be compute-bound if reuse is high enough.
evidence: Roofline definition: compute-bound when intensity > ridge; memory-bound when intensity < ridge. On-chip residency affects achieved intensity but is not the definition.
root_cause: Sufficient condition presented as definition.
correction: Say: 'A kernel is compute-bound when its arithmetic intensity exceeds the ridge point; keeping data on-chip is one way to raise intensity.'
acceptance_test: The definition matches the roofline criterion and does not equate on-chip residency with compute-bound.

page_hint: Ch 9 §6 (Architecture Consequence), anchors also in §3 Option A and §6 cost paragraph
quoted_clause: keeping the all-reduce on-node gives an ideal ring time about 11× below the assumed InfiniBand case and about 180× below the assumed RoCE case (§9.3)
observed: The chapter compares an eight-rank on-node NVLink all-reduce with eight-rank cross-node InfiniBand and Ethernet all-reduces, then uses the resulting 11×/180× ratios as if they were fabric alternatives for the same data-parallel training job. The same conflation appears in the cost paragraph: 'A cluster of 8‑GPU H100 servers (NVSwitch inside each node) is the highest upfront capital expenditure, but it delivers the lowest per-iteration communication time' versus 'A cluster connected by 200 GbE RoCE has lower capital cost but higher per-iteration communication time.'
evidence: The §9.3 example explicitly says the NVLink case is 'not a memory-feasible eight-replica training deployment' and is a communication-only comparison. A data-parallel job across eight nodes with eight GPUs per node spans 64 ranks, not eight ranks inside one host. NVLink inside a node and InfiniBand/RoCE between nodes are complementary layers, not mutually exclusive alternatives. The 11×/180× ratios therefore compare different group sizes and topology scopes, not two fabrics serving the same collective.
root_cause: The chapter treats 'on-node NVLink' and 'inter-node InfiniBand/RoCE' as alternative fabrics for one all-reduce, instead of distinguishing intra-node and inter-node portions of a hierarchical collective.
correction: Rewrite §6 to separate the two layers. State that an eight-node data-parallel job uses NVLink/NVSwitch for intra-node exchanges and InfiniBand/RoCE for inter-node exchanges; compare InfiniBand versus Ethernet only for the inter-node portion, and compare NVLink only for the intra-node portion. If the chapter wants to retain the 11×/180× numbers, label them explicitly as comparisons between an eight-rank single-host collective and an eight-rank cross-host collective, not as fabric choices for the same job. Remove or qualify the capex/opex paragraph so it does not imply that NVSwitch-inside-node and 200GbE RoCE are mutually exclusive cluster designs.
acceptance_test: A reader can explain why an eight-node, eight-GPU-per-node data-parallel all-reduce uses both NVLink and InfiniBand/RoCE, and cannot infer from §6 that replacing InfiniBand with NVLink inside each node eliminates the inter-node collective.

page_hint: Ch 9 §7 first bullet ('What We Still Don't Know')
quoted_clause: The benchmark numbers above assume a dedicated collective on a quiet fabric.
observed: The chapter's §9.3 numbers are analytical estimates, not benchmark measurements. §9.3 says 'These are analytical comparisons, not measured NCCL results'; Fig 9.1 says 'No curve is measured performance.' The §7 bullet nevertheless calls them 'benchmark numbers.'
evidence: The manuscript's own evidence labels and caveats contradict the phrase 'benchmark numbers.' This is an evidence-label error, not a numerical error.
root_cause: The uncertainty bullet was written as if §9.3 contained measurements, while the chapter deliberately presents analytical comparisons.
correction: Replace 'The benchmark numbers above' with 'The analytical estimates above' or 'The communication arithmetic above.' If the bullet intends to discuss real benchmark data, add a separate sentence identifying which measured results, if any, are being referenced.
acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 9 calls the §9.3 analytical estimates 'benchmark numbers' or otherwise implies they are measured results.

page_hint: Ch 9 §1, paragraph beginning 'The bandwidth each collective consumes...'
quoted_clause: the number of participating nodes (N)
observed: The text defines N as the number of participating nodes, but the chapter has just established that a rank is not a synonym for a server and that one server can host several ranks. The collective arithmetic in §9.3 uses N as the number of ranks in the ring, not the number of nodes.
evidence: The chapter's own definition says 'A rank is an index within a communication group, not a synonym for a server — one server can host several ranks.' The ring formula uses eight logical ranks, not eight nodes. Using 'nodes' for N creates a terminology drift that can produce wrong group-size arithmetic in multi-GPU nodes.
root_cause: The sentence uses 'nodes' where the collective model requires 'ranks' or 'participants.'
correction: Replace 'the number of participating nodes (N)' with 'the number of participating ranks (N)' or 'the number of participants in the collective (N).' Audit the surrounding paragraph and §9.3 for any other place where 'node' is used for a collective rank.
acceptance_test: Every use of N in Ch 9's collective arithmetic is explicitly a rank count or participant count, and no sentence defines N as a node count.

quoted_clause: The collective operations that dominate multi-node training and inference are:
observed: The list that follows contains all-reduce, all-gather, and reduce-scatter, but omits all-to-all. All-to-all is a dominant collective for MoE training and inference, and the chapter's own Table 9-2 includes it. The sentence therefore overstates the list's completeness.
evidence: Table 9-2 includes all-to-all and describes it as 'Redistribute a source-by-destination partition, as in expert routing.' Expert parallelism is a major multi-node training and inference pattern. A reader told that the three listed operations 'dominate' may under-budget all-to-all traffic in MoE systems.
root_cause: The list was scoped to the three collectives used in the chapter's ring arithmetic, but the sentence claims dominance across multi-node training and inference.
correction: Either add all-to-all to the list and explain its role in expert routing, or qualify the sentence: 'The three collectives used in this chapter's ring arithmetic are...' Do not claim that the list is the complete set of dominant multi-node collectives.
acceptance_test: The chapter either includes all-to-all in its 'dominant collectives' list or explicitly limits the list to the collectives used in its worked example.

quoted_clause: Measured effective bandwidth is typically 40–60% of peak [ILLUSTRATIVE]
observed: The sentence begins with PCIe Gen5 x16 but then states a general 'typically 40–60% of peak' figure without scoping it to PCIe, NVLink, InfiniBand, message size, or collective type. Modern NVLink and InfiniBand large-message collectives can achieve substantially higher fractions of peak; PCIe and small-message collectives can be lower.
evidence: The chapter itself distinguishes peak from achieved bandwidth and warns that message size and topology matter. A single 40–60% range across all fabrics is not supported by the chapter's own analysis and can mislead capacity planning.
root_cause: A PCIe-specific observation was generalized into a cross-fabric rule of thumb.
correction: Scope the range explicitly, e.g. 'For PCIe Gen5 x16 and small-to-medium collectives, measured effective bandwidth is often in the 40–60% range; NVLink and InfiniBand large-message collectives can achieve higher fractions, but must be measured.' Alternatively, remove the numeric range and keep the instruction to design against measured bandwidth.
acceptance_test: The Common Mistakes section does not state a universal 40–60% effective-bandwidth range without fabric, message-size, and collective-type qualifications.

quoted_clause: RoCE and InfiniBand use the same 64b/66b line coding but differ in framing and header sizes.
observed: The claim is overgeneralized. 200GbE and 400GbE Ethernet commonly use 256b/257b transcoding, not 64b/66b, and line coding varies by speed and PHY. InfiniBand's coding also varies by generation. The sentence presents a single coding scheme as common to both families.
evidence: The chapter is otherwise careful to distinguish standards, implementations, and physical layers. A blanket 'same 64b/66b line coding' statement collapses those distinctions and can produce incorrect payload-efficiency arithmetic at 200/400Gb/s.
root_cause: A low-speed Ethernet/InfiniBand coding detail was generalized across all current speeds.
correction: Replace the sentence with a speed-scoped statement, e.g. 'At the speeds discussed here, Ethernet and InfiniBand use different physical-layer coding and framing; use the specific standard's payload-efficiency figure rather than assuming a common 64b/66b overhead.' If the 64b/66b example is retained, label it as applying only to the specific 25/100Gb/s cases where it holds.
acceptance_test: The chapter no longer claims that RoCE and InfiniBand universally use the same 64b/66b line coding; any coding-efficiency example is tied to a specific speed and standard.

page_hint: Ch 9 §5, fourth and fifth Common Mistakes bullets
quoted_clause: the price per GB of optics and cables is 5–10× that of Ethernet [ILLUSTRATIVE] ... a 200 Gb/s RoCE2 link delivers ~180 Gb/s
observed: Two terminology/unit problems: 'price per GB of optics and cables' uses a storage-capacity unit for a cost comparison that should be per port, per cable, or per Gb/s; and 'RoCE2' is not the standard spelling of RoCEv2.
evidence: The surrounding discussion compares fabric cost and link throughput, not cost per gigabyte of stored data. 'RoCE2' appears twice in the same section and is inconsistent with the standard term 'RoCEv2.'
root_cause: Informal shorthand and a unit error survived copyediting.
correction: Replace 'price per GB of optics and cables' with 'price per port, cable, or Gb/s of optics and cables' and replace 'RoCE2' with 'RoCEv2' throughout.
acceptance_test: The cost comparison uses a dimensionally appropriate unit, and every occurrence of the protocol name is spelled 'RoCEv2.'

quoted_clause: Table 9-2 states the full set of operations this chapter's traffic arithmetic can encounter within one group.
observed: Table 9-2 includes Barrier, Reduce, Broadcast, and All-to-all, none of which appear in the chapter's traffic arithmetic. Barrier in particular has no byte-traffic arithmetic. The sentence overclaims the table's scope.
evidence: The chapter's worked example uses only reduce-scatter and all-gather within an all-reduce. Table 9-2 is a broader semantics reference, not the 'full set' encountered by the traffic arithmetic.
root_cause: The table was expanded beyond the arithmetic but the introductory sentence was not updated.
correction: Change to 'Table 9-2 summarizes the collective operations discussed in this chapter and the semantics that matter when interpreting their traffic.' Or explicitly separate the operations used in the arithmetic from the broader reference table.
acceptance_test: The sentence introducing Table 9-2 does not claim that every listed operation participates in the chapter's byte-traffic arithmetic.

page_hint: Ch 9 §8 mini-case, paragraph beginning 'Concretely, for the canonical 8×H100 host...'
quoted_clause: the meaningful per-step data movement is a TP all-reduce of the per-layer activations (tens of MBs, not GBs)
observed: The phrase 'tens of MBs' is presented without a batch-size or sequence-length assumption. For single-token decode at small batch, per-layer activation exchange can be kilobytes to low megabytes; for large batched decode it can reach tens of megabytes. The range is workload-dependent.
evidence: The chapter's own mental model makes activation size a function of batch, sequence length, hidden size, and dtype. A bare 'tens of MBs' can be misread as a property of the canonical host rather than of a particular operating point.
root_cause: A representative order-of-magnitude estimate was stated without its operating-point assumptions.
correction: Add the batch/sequence assumptions behind 'tens of MBs,' or replace with a scaling statement: 'per-layer activation exchange scales with batch × sequence length × hidden size × dtype; at the canonical operating point it is on the order of X.'
acceptance_test: The mini-case states the batch/sequence assumptions behind its activation-size estimate, or replaces the estimate with an explicit scaling relation.

page_hint: Ch 9 §8 mini-case, paragraph beginning 'In disaggregated serving...'
quoted_clause: exchanging activations or KV fragments is the normal case that fits comfortably within NVLink
observed: The 35 GB KV transfer is calculated at ~0.08 s over 450 GB/s, which is a lower bound and can be significant relative to TTFT or decode SLOs. 'Fits comfortably' is an unsupported qualitative conclusion.
evidence: The same paragraph gives the arithmetic: 35 GB ÷ 450 GB/s ≈ 0.08 s. Whether that is 'comfortable' depends on the SLO, the transfer path, and whether the transfer is on the critical path. The chapter elsewhere insists on measured paths and SLO-goodput.
root_cause: A bandwidth-feasibility statement was phrased as a latency-comfort statement.
correction: Replace 'fits comfortably within NVLink' with 'is bandwidth-feasible on NVLink in this idealized calculation; whether 0.08 s is acceptable depends on the TTFT/SLO budget and the measured transfer path.'
acceptance_test: The mini-case does not assert that a ~0.08 s KV transfer is 'comfortable' without tying that judgment to an explicit SLO or measured path.

quoted_clause: prefill is **compute-bound** ... decode is **bandwidth-bound**
observed: The text states the regimes as general properties of prefill and decode, not as first-order regimes for the canonical workload. The same unqualified framing recurs in the P/D definition, mental model, disaggregation section, and speculative-decoding common mistake.
evidence: Prefill can be memory- or communication-bound at short sequences, small batches, or low arithmetic intensity; decode can be compute-bound at large batch, long context, or high arithmetic intensity. The book's own roofline model requires model architecture, sequence length, batch/concurrency, precision, kernels, hardware, and serving configuration.
root_cause: A useful first-order regime was promoted to a universal law; the canonical workload's assumptions were dropped.
correction: Qualify every occurrence: 'for the canonical 9.2K/300 workload on 8×H100 with FP16 and the stated batch, prefill is compute-dominated and decode is bandwidth-dominated; this is a regime, not a law.' Add the conditions and a counterexample.
acceptance_test: Search all occurrences of 'prefill is compute-bound' and 'decode is bandwidth-bound'; each is either scoped to the canonical workload or accompanied by the conditions under which it fails. No unqualified universal remains.

quoted_clause: TTFT budget 1.2 s ... inflating TTFT toward the 2 s SLO breach
observed: The canonical workload sets a 1.2 s TTFT budget, but the discrete-batching paragraph compares TTFT to a 2 s SLO. If 2 s is an end-to-end SLO, the sentence conflates TTFT with end-to-end latency; if 2 s is the TTFT SLO, the 1.2 s budget is stale.
evidence: The two values are in the same worked example; no definition distinguishes them.
root_cause: Canonical SLO ledger not reconciled; TTFT and end-to-end latency mixed.
correction: State the canonical SLOs explicitly: TTFT ≤ 1.2 s, TPOT ≤ 25 ms, end-to-end ≤ 2 s (if that is the intent). Rewrite the discrete-batching sentence to use the correct metric and value.
acceptance_test: A single canonical SLO table lists TTFT, TPOT, and end-to-end; every worked example uses those values and names the metric.

quoted_clause: ideal utilization is ... ≈ 2.9× (out of 4×)
observed: 2.9× is an ideal speedup, not utilization. Utilization is 2.9/4 = 72.7% (or 32/44 = 72.7%). The same mislabel appears for 3.66×.
evidence: Formula gives speedup mP/(m+P−1); utilization = m/(m+P−1). For P=4,m=8, utilization = 8/11 = 72.7%, speedup = 32/11 = 2.91×.
root_cause: Speedup and utilization conflated.
correction: Call 32/11 an ideal speedup; report utilization separately as 8/11 ≈ 72.7% (or 32/44). Do the same for m=32: speedup 128/35 ≈ 3.66×, utilization 32/35 ≈ 91.4%.
acceptance_test: Every PP example labels speedup and utilization separately and the arithmetic matches the definitions.

quoted_clause: so P−1 stage-slots are wasted out of the m · P slots each stage would otherwise work
observed: The formula is correct, but the explanation is dimensionally wrong. The pipeline adds P−1 time slots to the makespan; each of P stages is idle for P−1 slots, so total idle stage-slots are P(P−1), not P−1. The bubble fraction of makespan is (P−1)/(m+P−1).
evidence: For P=4,m=8: makespan = 11 slots; each stage works 8, idle 3; total idle = 12 stage-slots; total capacity = 44; utilization = 32/44 = 72.7%.
root_cause: Time slots and stage-slots conflated.
correction: Rewrite: 'The pipeline makespan is m+P−1 stage-times instead of mP; the bubble is P−1 stage-times per stage, so utilization is m/(m+P−1).'
acceptance_test: The derivation of the bubble fraction and total idle stage-slots matches the formula.

quoted_clause: ~1.29 PFLOP → ~1.19 PFLOPS required over the ~1.08 s prefill budget, vs 0.989 PFLOPS peak
observed: 1.29/1.08 = 1.194 PFLOPS is the aggregate rate for one request. Comparing it to 0.989 PFLOPS (one H100's FP16 dense peak) is only valid if the request is served by one GPU. The canonical host is 8×H100 with aggregate peak ~7.91 PFLOPS; per-GPU required rate is ~0.149 PFLOPS. The sentence does not state which denominator is intended.
evidence: 8 × 0.989 = 7.912 PFLOPS. 1.194/8 = 0.149 PFLOPS per GPU. At 10 rps, aggregate prefill demand is 12.9 PFLOPS, which exceeds the node peak; that is the relevant capacity statement.
root_cause: Aggregate vs per-GPU vs per-node throughput mixed; concurrency omitted.
correction: State the basis explicitly: per request, 1.29 PFLOP over 1.08 s = 1.19 PFLOPS aggregate; on 8×H100 that is 0.149 PFLOPS/GPU vs 0.989 peak; at 10 rps the aggregate is 12.9 PFLOPS, so one node cannot sustain the canonical average without more replicas. Use the correct denominator for the claim.
acceptance_test: A dimensional ledger shows per-request FLOPs, per-request rate, per-GPU rate, per-node peak, and offered load; every comparison uses matching units and scope.

quoted_clause: the shard-invariant cause is the low ~1.0 FLOP/byte intensity
observed: The ~1.0 FLOP/byte figure is the batch-size-1 decode intensity for FP16 weights (2 FLOPs per parameter per token / 2 bytes per parameter). At the canonical continuous-batching concurrency, intensity is B × 1.0 FLOP/byte (before KV/attention traffic), so at B=16 it is ~16 FLOP/byte, not ~1.0. The text does not state the batch assumption.
evidence: Arithmetic intensity = 2B / bytes_per_param. For FP16, = B FLOP/byte. The H100 FP16 ridge point is ~989 TFLOPS / 3.35 TB/s ≈ 295 FLOP/byte, so decode can still be bandwidth-bound at B=16, but the stated 1.0 is not the serving operating point.
root_cause: Batch-size-1 roofline number used as a shard-invariant serving property.
correction: Write the batch-dependent formula, state the canonical batch/concurrency, and compute the actual intensity. Say 'at batch 1, ~1 FLOP/byte; at the canonical batch B, ~B FLOP/byte; still below the ridge point, so bandwidth-dominated, but not 1.0.'
acceptance_test: The roofline calculation includes batch size and matches the canonical serving concurrency; no unqualified 1.0 FLOP/byte claim remains.

quoted_clause: PagedAttention improves memory capacity by eliminating KV fragmentation.
observed: PagedAttention reduces external fragmentation and over-reservation by allocating fixed-size blocks; it does not eliminate fragmentation. Block-level internal fragmentation remains, and metadata/page-table overhead exists. It improves effective capacity utilization, not physical capacity.
evidence: Fixed-size blocks can waste up to block_size−1 slots per allocation; the book's own [S6] note says block-allocation/metadata overhead is not vendor-measured.
root_cause: Mechanism overstated as elimination.
correction: Say 'reduces external fragmentation and over-reservation, improving effective KV capacity; block-level internal fragmentation and metadata overhead remain.'
acceptance_test: No 'eliminating fragmentation' claim; the text distinguishes external vs internal fragmentation and capacity vs utilization.

quoted_clause: Prefix caching reduces memory capacity and prefill compute by reusing already-computed KV.
observed: Prefix caching consumes memory to store cached KV. It can reduce aggregate KV residency when many requests share a prefix, but it does not 'reduce memory capacity'; it trades cache memory for prefill compute and duplicate KV. The phrase is backwards.
evidence: A cached prefix occupies HBM; the benefit is avoiding duplicate KV and recomputation across requests. If the prefix is not reused, it is pure overhead.
root_cause: Resource trade-off described as a capacity reduction.
correction: Say 'Prefix caching trades cache memory for reduced prefill compute and, when prefixes are shared, reduced duplicate KV residency; it can also reduce effective capacity if hit rate is low.'
acceptance_test: The text states the memory cost and the hit-rate condition; no claim that prefix caching reduces physical memory capacity.

quoted_clause: so decode slots never sit idle
observed: Continuous batching reduces scheduler-induced idle slots but cannot guarantee no idle. Slots can be idle because no request is ready, KV capacity is exhausted, prefill is running, the scheduler enforces an SLO/admission policy, or the batch is limited by memory/communication.
evidence: The mechanism admits/evicts at each step; it does not create work. The chapter's own measurement section asks to track 'idle decode slots,' which contradicts 'never.'
root_cause: Mechanism benefit stated as a guarantee.
correction: Say 'can keep decode slots busier by refilling freed slots when requests are available; idle can still occur due to insufficient arrivals, KV capacity, prefill, or scheduling policy.'
acceptance_test: No 'never' claim; the text lists conditions under which idle remains and reconciles with the measurement section.

quoted_clause: while a long decode runs, the freed FLOPs are continuously refilled by new short requests
observed: Decode is described in the same chapter as bandwidth-bound. The resource freed by a finishing request is a decode slot and its share of memory-bandwidth demand, not 'FLOPs.' Using FLOPs here contradicts the resource model and can mislead about what continuous batching amortizes.
evidence: Continuous batching amortizes per-step weight reads across more sequences; it increases arithmetic intensity and bandwidth utilization. It does not primarily refill idle FLOPs.
