page_hint: Ch 15, §5 Common Mistakes, bullet 'Using scaled-dot-product attention without FlashAttention' (printed page not determinable from chunk)
quoted_clause: For long contexts (9,200+ tokens) the quadratic memory cost of SDPA (O(L²)) dominates the FLOP cost.
observed: This bullet asserts that SDPA's quadratic cost dominates the FLOP cost at 9.2K tokens. The chapter's own §3 computes the opposite: the attention term is ≈2.2×10¹⁴ FLOPs at L=9,200, which is ≈17% of the parameter-matmul FLOPs (2NL = 1.288×10¹⁵) and ≈15% of total forward FLOPs (case ii, 1.5099 PFLOP), and ≈8.6% / ≈8% under the causal triangle (case iii, 1.3989 PFLOP). A reader who trusts the bullet will conclude that attention FLOPs dominate long-context prefill, which the chapter's arithmetic refutes.
evidence: Independent rederivation from the chapter's own inputs: attention = 4·L²·d_model·n_layers = 4 × 9,200² × 8,192 × 80 = 2.2188×10¹⁴ FLOPs. Parameter matmul = 2 × 70×10⁹ × 9,200 = 1.288×10¹⁵. Ratio = 17.2%. Total = 1.5099×10¹⁵ → attention share = 14.7%. Causal triangle: 1.1094×10¹⁴ → 8.6% of 2NL, 7.9% of total. All three figures match §3 exactly, so the bullet is the outlier.
root_cause: The bullet conflates the memory-traffic argument (which is FlashAttention's actual motivation) with a FLOP-dominance claim, and was written without reconciling against §3's arithmetic. The two claims are also different in kind: bytes and FLOPs are not comparable without a machine-balance factor.
correction: Rewrite the bullet's first sentence to: 'For long contexts the quadratic *memory traffic* of SDPA — materializing the L×L score matrix — dominates its cost, while its FLOP cost is ≈15% of total forward FLOPs at 9.2K (§3; ≈8% under a causal mask). FlashAttention's gain is therefore an I/O gain, not a FLOP reduction.' Keep the rest of the bullet (it already says 'pays off specifically when memory-bound').
acceptance_test: The bullet's FLOP claim must equal §3's 15% (case ii) / 8% (case iii) figures; a reader who recomputes 4·L²·d·n_layers ÷ (2NL + attention) at L=9,200 must find the same number printed in the bullet, and no sentence in Ch 15 may claim attention dominates FLOPs at 9.2K.

page_hint: Ch 15, §8 mini-case (queueing-delay and throughput figures) and §4 Measurement ('A minimal benchmark runs 40 rps'); scope note at chapter head
quoted_clause: drops from 320 ms (single host, batch-1) to 140 ms (dual host, continuous batch), and token throughput rises from ~8.5K to 70,000 tokens/s
observed: The mini-case's operating point is physically inconsistent with the chapter's own capacity-deficit arithmetic. The mini-case inherits the deployment's traffic profile (12.5/50 rps) but quotes queueing delays and a serving throughput that cannot exist at that offered load on one or two hosts. §4's benchmark protocol has the same defect: it prescribes running 40 rps on the single host, which the chapter itself shows is 6.5× over the host's prefill ceiling.
evidence: Host prefill ceiling (linear-only, 100% MFU) = 7.912×10¹⁵ FLOP/s ÷ 1.4×10¹¹ FLOP/token = 56,514 tok/s. Offered prefill demand: 12.5 rps × 9,200 = 115,000 tok/s → 2.03× over; 50 rps → 460,000 tok/s → 8.14× over; 40 rps → 368,000 tok/s → 6.51× over (the chapter's own figure). Batch-1 single host: 9,200 tokens in 1.08 s → 0.93 rps capacity vs 12.5 rps offered → 13.4× over, so a p95 queueing delay of 320 ms is impossible (the queue grows without bound). Offered token rate at 12.5 rps = 115,000 + 3,750 = 118,750 tok/s vs a two-host ceiling of 113,000 tok/s (linear-only) → the quoted 70,000 tok/s is *below* offered demand, i.e. the system is not keeping up. Under the alternative reading (a saturation test), queueing delay is unbounded, not 140 ms. Both readings fail.
root_cause: The mini-case never states the offered load of the benchmark it reports. It borrows the deployment's traffic profile for context while quoting numbers that are only coherent at a much lower load, and the §4 protocol was written before the chapter established the 6.5× prefill deficit.
correction: State the benchmark's offered load explicitly in both §4 and §8, and reconcile the numbers with the deficit arithmetic. Either (a) re-label the mini-case as a saturation/sweep test with the offered load stated and the queueing-delay figures marked as measured under saturation, or (b) re-derive the 320/140 ms and 8.5K/70,000 figures at a load the host can actually sustain (≤ ~2 rps for one host, ≤ ~4 rps for two). In §4, replace 'runs 40 rps' with a load the host can serve, or state explicitly that the 40 rps run is a saturation test whose queue is expected to grow.
acceptance_test: Every throughput and latency figure in §4 and §8 carries an explicit offered load; recomputing prefill demand ÷ host ceiling at that load yields ≤1, or the text explicitly states the system is saturated and the queue unbounded. A reader must not be able to compute a 13× overload next to a 320 ms p95 queueing delay.

page_hint: Ch 15, 'Two Mechanisms, Read as Mechanisms' → 'Speculative decoding' paragraph; and the Optimization Decision Map row 'high TPOT/ITL + HBM bandwidth saturated'
quoted_clause: quantization, batching up, speculative decoding, smaller active params, more bandwidth
observed: The chapter never states the condition under which speculative decoding actually reduces weight-stream traffic, and the decision map places it in precisely the regime where it does not help. Decode at batch B streams the full weight set once per step, so bytes/token = W/B. Speculative decoding with acceptance length k streams the weights once per k+1 tokens, so bytes/token = W/(k+1). The traffic saving is positive only when k+1 > B. At the chapter's own batch-32 test point (§4) with a typical k of 4, speculative decoding reduces bytes/token by zero while adding draft-model cost and verification overhead. This also puts the map in direct tension with §6, which recommends continuous batching (large B) as the primary decode lever.
evidence: W = 140 GB (FP16 70B). Batch-32 decode: 140/32 = 4.4 GB/token. Speculative with k=4: 140/5 = 28 GB/token — worse than batch-32 decode. Batch-1 decode: 140 GB/token vs 28 GB/token — a 5× saving. The saving therefore exists only in the low-batch regime, which is the opposite of the 'HBM bandwidth saturated' symptom the map attaches it to.
root_cause: The speculative-decoding mechanism was described in isolation from the batch dimension that the same chapter makes central, and the decision map's 'evidence / measurement' column omits decode batch size, so the reader cannot see the precondition.
correction: Add the batch condition to the mechanism paragraph: 'The saving exists only while the decode batch is smaller than the expected acceptance length k+1: at batch B the weights are already streamed once per step for B sequences (W/B bytes per token), so speculative decoding can only help when k+1 > B. At large batch, where the chapter's own continuous-batching recommendation puts the system, speculative decoding reduces weight traffic by nothing and adds draft cost.' Add 'current decode batch size vs expected acceptance length' to the map's evidence column and annotate the row accordingly.
acceptance_test: The mechanism paragraph contains the inequality k+1 > B (or an equivalent statement); the map's evidence column lists decode batch size; a reader must be able to conclude from the chapter alone that speculative decoding does not help at batch 32.

page_hint: Ch 15, §3 Worked Example, 'Attention FLOP comparison' paragraph
quoted_clause: Attention is two matmuls per token per head — Q·$K^{T}$ then ·V — each a multiply-accumulate of L²·d, so in FLOPs (2 per MAC) the per-layer cost is ≈ 4 × L² × d_model
observed: The derivation is mis-stated. For a single query token, Q·Kᵀ is (1×d)·(d×L) = L·d MACs and (QKᵀ)·V is (1×L)·(L×d) = L·d MACs, i.e. 4·L·d FLOPs per token per head. L²·d is the cost for all L query positions in one head, not per token. The final formula 4·L²·d_model per layer is correct, but it does not follow from the sentence as written, and a reader following the printed derivation literally gets a factor of L wrong.
evidence: Per token per head: 2 matmuls × L·d MACs × 2 FLOPs/MAC = 4·L·d = 4 × 9,200 × 128 = 4.71×10⁶ FLOPs. Across L tokens and 64 heads: 4·L²·d_model = 4 × 9,200² × 8,192 = 2.773×10¹² per layer — matches the printed ≈2.8×10¹². Per-head sequence figure 4 × 9,200² × 128 = 4.33×10¹⁰ also matches the printed ≈4.3×10¹⁰. So only the 'per token' qualifier is wrong.
root_cause: The derivation sentence was written at the sequence level but labeled per token; the correct per-token and per-sequence quantities were never separated.
correction: Rewrite: 'Attention is two matmuls per head — Q·Kᵀ then ·V — each L²·d MACs for the whole sequence (equivalently 4·L·d FLOPs per token per head); with 2 FLOPs per MAC and n_heads heads, the per-layer cost is 4·L²·d_model.'
acceptance_test: A reader following the printed derivation reproduces 4·L²·d_model per layer with no factor-of-L discrepancy, and the per-token and per-sequence quantities are separately stated.

page_hint: Ch 15, chapter title; §1 Concept; §4 heading 'Goodput vs. Batch Size: the Cache Lever'; §6; §8
quoted_clause: The serving system must therefore optimize three inter-dependent quantities: token throughput (tokens/s), per-token latency, and GPU memory utilization.
observed: The chapter is titled 'From "It Works" to "It Meets the SLO"' and uses 'goodput' and 'SLO' repeatedly (§4 heading and caption, §6 'measured goodput/latency knee', §8, decision-map 'SLO miss %'), but never defines goodput, never states the canonical SLO the chapter measures against (no TTFT target, no TPOT/ITL target), and §1's list of three optimized quantities omits SLO-goodput entirely — substituting raw throughput, which the book elsewhere insists is the wrong objective. A reader arriving at this chapter cannot tell what 'meeting the SLO' means numerically.
evidence: Occurrences of 'goodput' in Ch 15: §4 subsection heading, Fig 15.2 caption ('decode goodput vs batch size'), §4 prose ('batching raises decode goodput'), §6 ('measured goodput/latency knee'), §8. Occurrences of 'SLO': chapter title, §4, §5, §6, decision map. No definition sentence for either term appears in the chunk.
root_cause: The chapter was drafted as a mechanism survey; the SLO framing was added to the title and to the decision map without a corresponding definition or target statement.
correction: Add one short paragraph in §1 or §2 that (a) defines goodput as SLO-meeting tokens or requests per second, distinguishing it from raw throughput, and (b) states the canonical SLO the chapter uses (TTFT target and TPOT/ITL target) with an explicit cross-reference to the chapter where it is set. Add SLO-goodput to §1's list of the three quantities the serving system optimizes.
acceptance_test: A reader who has read only Ch 15 can state the chapter's goodput definition and the canonical TTFT/TPOT targets, and can explain why raw throughput is not the objective.

page_hint: Ch 15, §4 Measurement (first paragraph) vs. the Optimization Decision Map 'evidence / measurement' column
quoted_clause: we instrument the serving stack with three metric families: (a) token latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99) per request type, (b) GPU utilization (SM active, memory bandwidth via Nsight), and (c) KV cache size over time.
observed: The instrumentation list does not cover the evidence the chapter's own decision map requires. The map's 'evidence / measurement' column names: FLOP utilization, prefill queue depth, prefix-cache hit rate, HBM bandwidth utilization, effective bytes/token, KV bytes/token, context distribution, fragmentation, active sequences, attention kernel memory traffic vs compute, SLO miss %, token-size variance, queue depth, mixed-workload p99, phase-locked stalls, collective time, TP/PP/EP balance, placement. Of these, only FLOP/HBM utilization and KV size are covered by the three families. The chapter therefore tells the reader to diagnose with evidence it never says to collect.
evidence: Direct column-by-column comparison of §4's three metric families against the map's seven evidence cells.
root_cause: The decision map was authored independently of the instrumentation list; the two were never reconciled.
correction: Extend §4's metric list to cover the map's evidence column — at minimum add queue depth (prefill and decode), prefix-cache hit rate, SLO-compliance rate, effective bytes/token, and KV fragmentation/active-sequence count — or add a column to the map naming the metric family that produces each evidence item.
acceptance_test: Every evidence item in the decision map maps to a named instrumented metric in §4; no evidence cell requires a metric the chapter never mentions.

page_hint: Ch 15, §4 Measurement, final paragraph (after Fig 15.2) and its footnote [^oct-ccl-proxy]
quoted_clause: Summing all collective durations can overstate exposed cost when operations overlap. Subtracting every overlapped duration can understate cost when communication slows concurrent compute. The measured quantity is the change in the end-to-end critical path, supported by compute and communication traces. CPU progress threads, HBM, device links and NICs remain shared resources even when their work appears in separate profiler lanes.[^oct-ccl-proxy]
observed: A paragraph on NCCL collective-duration accounting, with a footnote citing NCCL's src/proxy.cc, sits inside the Measurement section of a chapter whose declared scope is single-host performance engineering. There is no antecedent for it, no collective, TP, or multi-GPU content anywhere else in the chapter, and it interrupts the goodput/batch-size subsection it is appended to. The footnote identifier 'oct-ccl-proxy' and the NCCL source indicate the paragraph originated in a distributed/collective chapter and was pasted in during restructuring without repairing the section boundary.
evidence: Full-chunk scan of Ch 15: no occurrence of tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, expert parallelism, NCCL, or collective outside this paragraph and the decision map's last row. The chapter's scope note explicitly frames the chapter around one 8×H100 host.
root_cause: Content migrated between chapters during restructuring; the surrounding subsection boundary and the footnote placement were not repaired.
correction: Move the paragraph and its footnote to the chapter that covers collectives and multi-GPU execution, with a cross-reference back if needed. If it must remain in Ch 15, add a one-sentence bridge ('multi-GPU collectives are profiled the same way — see Ch 18') and move the footnote marker with the text it annotates.
acceptance_test: §4 contains no paragraph whose subject matter is absent from the chapter; the NCCL footnote appears in the same section as its marker; the chapter's scope note and its content agree.

page_hint: Ch 15, §6 Architecture Consequence (decision 3) vs. chapter-head Scope note and §8 mini-case fleet screens
quoted_clause: on-host concurrency rises from ~17.5 to ~35.0 full-context users (436 GB ÷ 12.45 GB)
observed: §6 recommends FP8 KV quantization as a standing architecture decision, which doubles KV-resident slots per host from 17 to 35. The chapter's own fleet screens — 21 hosts at 40 rps and 26 hosts at 50 rps — are computed with the FP16 slot count of 17 and are never reconciled with the recommendation. The chapter therefore recommends a change that would roughly halve the fleet counts it quotes two paragraphs earlier, without saying so.
evidence: 436 GB ÷ 12.45 GB = 35.0 slots (FP8 KV). At 40 rps: ⌈344/17⌉ = 21 hosts (quoted) vs ⌈344/35⌉ = 10 hosts (FP8). At 50 rps: ⌈430/17⌉ = 26 hosts (quoted) vs ⌈430/35⌉ = 13 hosts (FP8). Under FP8 KV the prefill-compute requirement becomes binding instead: ⌈5.152×10¹⁶ / 7.912×10¹⁵⌉ = 7 hosts at 40 rps, so the FP8 fleet is bounded below by ~10 hosts, not 21.
root_cause: The fleet screens were computed from the canonical FP16 KV reference and were not re-run after the chapter's own recommendation was added; the two live in different sections with no cross-reference.
correction: State explicitly that the fleet screens use the FP16 KV reference, and add the FP8-KV variant with the note that prefill compute then becomes the binding constraint (⌈344/35⌉ = 10 hosts at 40 rps, bounded below by the ~7-host prefill requirement). Alternatively, make the fleet screens use the recommended configuration and note the FP16 baseline.
acceptance_test: Every host-count figure in Ch 15 states its KV-precision assumption; the FP8 variant appears at least once; a reader can see which of the two constraints binds under each precision.

page_hint: Ch 15, Table 15-1 'Dominant Bottleneck' column (Light and Peak rows) vs. §3 Worked Example peak analysis
observed: The bottleneck column is not derived from the chapter's own arithmetic and contradicts §3 in two ways. (a) The Peak row ('KV + Inter-GPU bandwidth') omits the prefill compute deficit, which §3 identifies as the primary peak signal (6.5× over host peak), and introduces 'Inter-GPU bandwidth', a bottleneck this chapter never analyzes — there is no TP, collective, or multi-GPU content in Ch 15. (b) The Light row's 'Compute (SDPA)' is hard to reconcile: at 2 rps the prefill demand is only ~33% of the host's FP16 peak, while 17 in-flight requests × 24.9 GB = 423 GB ≈ 97% of the 436 GB KV budget — KV, not compute, is the binding constraint even in the 'light' regime. The table's own note claims the column 'reflects the roofline logic of Chapter 8', which the numbers do not support.
evidence: Light: prefill demand = 2 × 9,200 × 1.4×10¹¹ = 2.576×10¹⁵ FLOP/s ÷ 7.912×10¹⁵ = 0.33× of host peak; KV demand = 17 × 24.9 GB = 423.3 GB ÷ 436 GB = 0.97× of the KV budget. Typical: prefill 1.63×, KV 86 × 24.9 = 2,141 GB ÷ 436 = 4.91×. Peak: prefill 6.51×, KV 344 × 24.9 = 8,566 GB ÷ 436 = 19.6×. The prefill ratio is the quantity that rises monotonically and is the one §3 argues about; the table's bottleneck labels do not track it.
root_cause: The bottleneck column was filled in by narrative shape (compute → KV → KV+inter-GPU) rather than derived from the two ratios the chapter already computes, and 'Inter-GPU bandwidth' was imported from a different chapter's vocabulary.
correction: Re-derive each row's bottleneck from the two ratios the chapter already computes and print them as columns: 'Prefill demand ÷ host peak' (0.33× / 1.63× / 6.51×) and 'KV demand ÷ host KV budget' (0.97× / 4.91× / 19.6×). Then label the bottleneck from those ratios: KV capacity binds in all three regimes on a single host, with the prefill compute deficit becoming binding at peak. Remove 'Inter-GPU bandwidth' from this table or replace it with the prefill compute deficit.
acceptance_test: For each row, the printed bottleneck follows from a printed ratio; the Light row shows both a compute ratio below 1 and a KV ratio near 1; no bottleneck named in the table is absent from the chapter's analysis.

quoted_clause: (1) FlashAttention‑2 as the default attention kernel, fused with RoPE and QKV projection to minimize HBM transactions
observed: FlashAttention-2 is an attention kernel: it takes Q, K, V as inputs and performs tiled attention with an online softmax. It does not fuse the QKV projection GEMM or the RoPE application into the attention kernel in its standard form. The sentence conflates attention-kernel fusion with GEMM-level fusion and with a separate RoPE-fusion choice, and it contradicts §3's careful framing of FlashAttention as an attention-I/O mechanism (tiling, online softmax, no materialized L×L matrix).
evidence: §3's own description of FlashAttention contains no projection or RoPE fusion; the chapter's Fig 15.1 caption likewise describes only tiled attention with online softmax. The QKV-projection fusion and the RoPE fusion are separate engineering choices made by the serving engine around the attention kernel.
root_cause: Conflation of 'fused attention' with 'fused attention + fused QKV GEMM + fused RoPE', which are three distinct decisions with distinct effects on HBM traffic.
correction: Split the decision into its components: '(1) FlashAttention-2 as the default attention kernel (attention-I/O fusion: tiled, online softmax, no materialized L×L score matrix); separately, fuse the three QKV projections into a single GEMM, and fuse RoPE into the attention prologue where the engine supports it.'
acceptance_test: The decision names which component performs each fusion; no sentence attributes QKV-projection or RoPE fusion to FlashAttention-2 itself; the description matches §3's account of the kernel.

quoted_clause: the single-host upper end is capped at the 100%-MFU ceiling, 7.91 ×10¹⁵ FLOP/s ÷ (2 ×70×10⁹ FLOP/token) ≈ 56,500 tok/s
observed: The ceiling is computed with the linear-only 2N FLOP/token convention (case i), which the chapter's own §3 shows omits the attention term — ≈15% of total forward FLOPs at the canonical 9,200-token context. At that context the true 100%-MFU ceiling is ≈49,000 tok/s, so the 'illustrative ~35,000–56,000 tokens/s' range's upper end sits above the achievable ceiling at the canonical context length. The convention is not stated at the point of use, even though §3 carefully enumerates cases (i)/(ii)/(iii).
evidence: Attention FLOPs per token at L=9,200 = 4·L²·d·n_layers / L = 2.2188×10¹⁴ / 9,200 = 2.412×10¹⁰ FLOP/token. Total per token = 1.4×10¹¹ + 2.412×10¹⁰ = 1.6412×10¹¹. Ceiling = 7.912×10¹⁵ / 1.6412×10¹¹ = 48,200 tok/s (≈49,000). The printed 56,500 is the context-free linear-only bound.
root_cause: The ceiling was computed with case (i) while §3 established cases (ii) and (iii); the convention is carried in §3 but dropped here.
correction: State the convention and give the context-aware ceiling: 'the single-host upper end is capped by the 100%-MFU ceiling: 7.91×10¹⁵ FLOP/s ÷ 1.4×10¹¹ FLOP/token ≈ 56,500 tok/s under the linear-only case (i); at the canonical 9,200-token context the attention term (§3, case ii) lowers this to ≈48,000 tok/s.'
acceptance_test: The ceiling figure names its FLOP convention and is consistent with §3's case (i)/(ii)/(iii) accounting; the stated achievable range's upper end does not exceed the context-aware ceiling.

quoted_clause: The MFU stabilizes at ~62 % — 70,000 tok/s × 2 × 70×10⁹ FLOP/token = 9.8 ×10¹⁵ FLOP/s against the two-host 15.82 ×10¹⁵ FLOP/s peak
observed: Same convention omission as the §6 ceiling: the 62% is computed with the linear-only 2N FLOP/token convention. At the canonical 9,200-token context the attention term adds ≈17% relative, giving ≈73% of peak under case (ii). The chapter elsewhere insists on naming the convention (case i/ii/iii in §3), so the omission here is an internal inconsistency rather than a stylistic choice, and it makes the mini-case's headline MFU understate achieved utilization by roughly a sixth.
evidence: 70,000 × (1.4×10¹¹ + 2.412×10¹⁰) = 1.149×10¹⁶ FLOP/s; two-host peak = 2 × 7.912×10¹⁵ = 1.5824×10¹⁶; ratio = 72.6%. The printed 9.8×10¹⁵ / 15.82×10¹⁵ = 61.9% is correct for case (i) only.
root_cause: The FLOP convention established in §3 was not carried into the mini-case arithmetic, and the mini-case's throughput is a mixed prefill+decode aggregate whose attention share depends on the mix, which is not stated.
correction: Label the convention in the sentence ('case (i), linear-only') and add the case-(ii) value: '≈62% under the linear-only convention; ≈73% including the attention term at 9.2K context (§3, case ii)'. State that the aggregate mixes prefill and decode and that the attention share depends on the phase mix.
acceptance_test: Every MFU figure in Ch 15 names its FLOP convention; a reader recomputing the mini-case's MFU with the §3 case-(ii) per-token cost finds the alternative value printed alongside.

quoted_clause: when many users share similar prompt prefixes, the KV cache can be partially shared, reducing memory traffic
observed: Prefix reuse eliminates redundant prefill computation and redundant KV allocation for the shared prefix. It does not reduce the KV bytes that must be read from HBM during decode for that prefix — decode reads the full K/V history of every sequence at every step regardless of whether the prefix was computed or reused. As written, the sentence can lead the reader to expect a decode-time bandwidth saving from prefix caching, which is the mechanism the chapter elsewhere (decision map, §6) correctly attributes to batching and quantization.
evidence: Decode attention reads the sequence's entire K/V history per step; the prefix's K/V must be resident and read whether it was just computed or restored from a cache. The savings from prefix reuse are (a) prefill FLOPs for the shared prefix and (b) KV capacity for the shared prefix.
root_cause: Conflation of 'avoid recomputation' with 'avoid re-reading', a distinction the chapter's own §4 measurement paragraph makes elsewhere ('compare the bytes transferred per request').
correction: Rewrite: 'when many users share similar prompt prefixes, the shared prefix's KV need not be recomputed or re-allocated, which removes prefill FLOPs and KV capacity; the KV bytes for that prefix are still read during decode, so the saving is in compute and capacity, not in decode-time traffic.'
acceptance_test: The sentence names prefill FLOPs and KV capacity as the savings and makes no claim about a decode-time traffic reduction; the claim is consistent with the decision map's placement of prefix caching under prefill.

quoted_clause: A minimal benchmark runs 40 rps with warm‑up, records the p95 token latency, and measures the GPU memory fraction consumed by KV cache.
observed: 'p95 token latency' is ambiguous between per-token generation latency (TPOT/ITL) and per-request latency, in a chapter that elsewhere distinguishes TTFT, TPOT, queueing delay and end-to-end latency precisely (the mini-case separates 'p95 queueing/scheduling delay' from TTFT).
evidence: The chapter uses 'token latency' here and 'per-token latency' in §1, while the mini-case and decision map use TTFT/TPOT/ITL. Three different terms for overlapping quantities.
correction: Replace with 'records p95 TTFT and p95 TPOT/ITL separately, plus p95 queueing delay'.
acceptance_test: No bare 'token latency' remains in Ch 15 where TTFT, TPOT/ITL, or queueing delay is the intended quantity.

quoted_clause: one often sees a FlashAttention‑class kernel reported at a *different achieved HBM bandwidth* than a naive SDPA kernel (illustratively ~150 GB/s vs ~400 GB/s for 9,500‑token contexts)
observed: 'one often sees' asserts a recurring observation in the literature with no citation, and the illustrative values (150 / 400 GB/s) are roughly 4–12% of the H100's ~3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth, which a reader may misread as typical achieved bandwidth on this hardware. The pedagogical point (a rate is not a byte count) is correct and worth keeping; the framing is what is weak.
evidence: H100 SXM HBM3 bandwidth ≈ 3.35 TB/s (Chapter 8 canonical hardware). 150 GB/s ≈ 4.5% of peak; 400 GB/s ≈ 12% of peak. Neither figure is attributed to a measurement.
correction: Either cite a specific measurement, or reframe as hypothetical: 'a FlashAttention-class kernel may report a *lower* achieved HBM bandwidth than a naive SDPA kernel precisely because it is no longer bandwidth-limited — in a hypothetical profile, 150 GB/s vs 400 GB/s against the H100's ~3.35 TB/s peak.'
acceptance_test: The claim carries a source or is explicitly hypothetical, and the reader can see the ratio of the quoted rates to the device's peak bandwidth.

quoted_clause: FlashAttention fuses read‑write‑compute and reduces HBM traffic by ~3–5× ([ILLUSTRATIVE] — kernel‑ and length‑dependent; measure bytes/request on the target stack)
observed: The factor is stated without a baseline and without a source. The comparison baseline is decisive: against a naive SDPA that materializes the L×L score matrix, the traffic reduction is dominated by the elimination of that intermediate (a much larger effect than 3–5×); against a well-written fused baseline it is far smaller. §3 and Fig 15.1 describe the saving as the elimination of materialized-intermediate traffic, so the three framings of 'the FlashAttention traffic benefit' in the chapter are not reconciled. The chapter also warns against quoting published speedups, so quoting an unsourced traffic factor cuts against its own standard.
evidence: §3: 'the materialized-intermediate traffic is what drops'; Fig 15.1 caption: 'far fewer HBM round-trips'; §5: 'reduces HBM traffic by ~3–5×'. Three different magnitudes for the same mechanism, none cross-referenced.
correction: State the baseline explicitly and either cite the FlashAttention I/O analysis already referenced in Fig 15.1 (arXiv:2205.14135) or reframe the range as a target-stack measurement: 'reduces bytes/request by a factor that depends entirely on the baseline — against a naive SDPA that materializes the L×L score matrix the saving is dominated by the eliminated intermediate; against an already-fused baseline it is small.'
acceptance_test: The traffic factor is accompanied by its baseline and either a source or an explicit measurement label; the magnitudes quoted in §3, §4 and §5 are mutually consistent or explicitly distinguished by baseline.

page_hint: Ch 15, §5 Common Mistakes, FlashAttention bullet, final sentence
quoted_clause: for moderate lengths (2,000–4,000 tokens) the HBM bandwidth reduction typically translates to a ~1.3–1.8× throughput gain on H100 (illustrative — bench the specific kernel on the target hardware)
observed: 'typically' asserts a general behavior for a range the same sentence labels illustrative; the parenthetical does not neutralize the adverb. This is the kind of wording the book's own claim-strength discipline elsewhere avoids.
evidence: The sentence carries both 'typically' and '[illustrative]', which are in tension.
correction: Replace 'typically translates to' with 'can translate to', or move the range into a clearly labeled scenario table.
acceptance_test: No 'typically', 'always', or 'never' attaches to an ILLUSTRATIVE range anywhere in Ch 15.

page_hint: Ch 15, §6 Architecture Consequence decision (2) and §7 open question 2
quoted_clause: (2) continuous batching, with the maximum chunk size chosen empirically from the measured goodput/latency knee
observed: 'Chunk size' is used for two different engine parameters: the continuous-batching iteration granularity (how many decode steps or sequences are grouped per scheduler iteration) and the chunked-prefill token budget (how many prompt tokens are processed per prefill chunk). The chapter's own 'Chunked prefill' mechanism section defines the latter; §6 and §7 use the term in the former sense without saying so. §7's open question ('the optimal continuous-batch chunk size') inherits the ambiguity and is therefore not answerable as written.
evidence: §6 'Chunked prefill' paragraph: 'splits that prefill into smaller pieces and interleaves them with decode steps'; §6 decision (2): 'continuous batching, with the maximum chunk size'; §7: 'the optimal continuous-batch chunk size'. Two distinct parameters, one label.
correction: Name them distinctly throughout — e.g. 'decode-step iteration granularity' and 'chunked-prefill token budget' — and rewrite §7's question to name the parameter it asks about.
acceptance_test: A reader can tell which engine parameter each mention of 'chunk' refers to; §7's open question names a specific parameter.

page_hint: Ch 15, §5 Common Mistakes, 'Ignoring KV cache growth' bullet
quoted_clause: A 70B model with 9,500‑token contexts consumes ≈24.9 GB of KV per user (≈2.62 MB/token × 9,500, max end‑of‑generation)
observed: KV is a per-sequence (per-request) quantity, not a per-user one. §3 explicitly draws this distinction ('~86 is the *request occupancy*, distinct from the ~100 *active-user* population'), and the same bullet then says '100 concurrent full-context users', reintroducing the conflation the chapter elsewhere warns against. The bullet also drops §3's qualifier that the 80-layer/8,192-hidden geometry is 'the 70B-class teaching model, not a universal 70B property'.
evidence: §3: 'the canonical full-MHA reference geometry (80 layers, hidden dimension 8,192 — the 70B-class teaching model, not a universal 70B property)'. §5 states the same 24.9 GB figure with no such qualifier and with 'per user'.
correction: Use 'per in-flight request (per sequence)' throughout the bullet, change '100 concurrent full-context users' to '100 concurrent full-context requests', and restore the geometry qualifier.
acceptance_test: The bullet uses 'request'/'sequence' wherever it means a KV allocation, and retains the 'not a universal 70B property' qualifier.

quoted_clause: A fourth decision, borne out of the mini‑case (Ch11 §11.8), is to design the request‑routing layer for KV cache affinity
observed: The mini-case does not bear out this decision; it ends by raising it as an open question ('The remaining question is whether the cross-host request routing layer can maintain affinity KV cache residency') and labels the affinity gain and cold-start cost as [ILLUSTRATIVE SCENARIO RESULT]. The claim strength ('borne out of') exceeds the evidence the chapter itself supplies.
evidence: §8 final sentences: 'The remaining question is whether the cross-host request routing layer can maintain affinity KV cache residency... The ∼20 % affinity throughput gain and the ∼2.1 s cold-start warm-up cost are themselves [ILLUSTRATIVE SCENARIO RESULT] values, not measured results.'
correction: Rewrite as: 'A fourth decision, raised by the mini-case (Ch11 §11.8) but not yet validated, is to design the request-routing layer for KV cache affinity.'
acceptance_test: The decision's justification matches the mini-case's own conclusion; no architecture decision in Ch 15 is described as 'borne out' by an illustrative scenario.

page_hint: Ch 15, Optimization Decision Map table (mechanisms column, rows 1 and 3) and the paragraph immediately following the table
quoted_clause: prefix caching, chunked prefill, faster/batched kernels, more compute, P/D separation
observed: Three inconsistencies in the map's mechanism column. (a) Weight quantization is discussed in the prose immediately after the map — with the chapter's only bottleneck-shift warning — but appears in no row, although it is the one mechanism the prose singles out. (b) Chunked prefill is listed under 'prefill compute', but the chapter's own mechanism section defines it as a scheduling mechanism that bounds the per-phase burst and reduces decode interference; it does not reduce prefill FLOPs, so it does not address a compute-saturated prefill. (c) GQA/MQA is listed among runtime levers with only the hedge '(if model allows)'; it is a model-architecture choice requiring different weights, different quality, and a different fleet, not a serving-system knob.
evidence: §5 'Chunked prefill' paragraph: 'splits that prefill into smaller pieces and interleaves them with decode steps... a scheduling mechanism to bound the per-phase burst'. Post-table paragraph: 'Weight quantization is a candidate intervention when weight capacity or weight traffic is limiting. After the change, the bottleneck may move to KV access, attention, collective communication, conversion kernels or queueing.'
root_cause: The map and the surrounding prose were authored as separate artifacts and never reconciled; the map also mixes model-architecture choices with runtime mechanisms without distinguishing them.
correction: Add a weight-quantization row (symptom: weight capacity or weight traffic limiting; evidence: weight bytes read per token, checkpoint size vs achieved throughput; trade-off: quality loss, conversion kernels, bottleneck shift). Move chunked prefill to the 'prefill and decode interfering' row. Annotate GQA/MQA as 'requires a different model — not a runtime change; entails different weights, quality, and fleet'.
acceptance_test: Every mechanism named in the prose appears in the map; each map mechanism's row matches the mechanism's own definition elsewhere in the chapter; model-architecture choices are visually distinguished from runtime levers.

page_hint: Ch 15, Table 15-1, column 'Illustrative load pressure (dimensionless labeled score)' and its explanatory note
quoted_clause: Illustrative load pressure (dimensionless labeled score)
observed: The column's own note concedes it has 'no FLOP numerator or denominator behind it' and is 'ordinal and scenario-chosen', yet it occupies a numeric column in a table whose other four numeric columns are all computed quantities with stated derivations. Readers will anchor on 12/38/52 and may compare them with numbers elsewhere in the book. The note's defence of the column is longer than the information the column carries.
evidence: The chapter already computes two well-defined ratios per regime that would make the column informative: prefill demand ÷ host peak = 0.33× / 1.63× / 6.51×, and KV demand ÷ host KV budget = 0.97× / 4.91× / 19.6×.
correction: Replace the load-pressure column with the two defined ratios (or with one of them plus the binding constraint), and delete the paragraph defending the ordinal score. If the ordinal score is retained for teaching shape, move it out of the numeric table into prose.

quoted_clause: the dominant cost in LLM inference is the arithmetic intensity of transformer matrix multiplications and the memory bandwidth consumed by KV cache reads and writes on every token step
observed: Arithmetic intensity is a ratio (FLOP/byte), not a cost. The sentence names a property of the workload as a cost term, in the chapter's opening concept section — the first substantive claim the reader meets. The chapter's own §3 goes to some length to distinguish kernel regime from workload capacity deficit, so the imprecision is out of step with the rest of the chapter.
evidence: The same section later says 'the architect's first move is to identify which resource—compute, bandwidth, or latency—is the primary constraint', which is the correct framing.
correction: Rewrite: 'the dominant cost in LLM inference is the FLOPs executed by transformer matrix multiplications and the memory bandwidth consumed by KV cache reads and writes on every token step; the arithmetic intensity of each phase determines which of those two dominates.'
acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 15 calls a ratio a cost; the Concept section's framing matches §3's regime vocabulary.

page_hint: Ch 15, 'The Architect's Question' opening paragraph and the Scope note immediately following it
quoted_clause: how do we configure an 8×H100 host to serve a 70B parameter model at 40 requests-per-second peak while keeping per-request latency within a target budget
observed: The chapter's driving question is disclaimed by its own scope note two sentences later ('not a claim that one host absorbs the 40 rps peak'). The reader is asked a question the chapter says it will not answer, which weakens the framing that is supposed to orient the whole chapter.
evidence: Scope note: 'the 8×H100 host here is the *per-request feasibility container* — does one host meet one request's latency and memory SLO? — **not** a claim that one host absorbs the 40 rps peak.'
correction: Restate the question to match the scope: 'what does it take for one 8×H100 host to meet one request's latency and memory SLO for a 70B model, and what does that imply for the fleet required at 40 rps?'
acceptance_test: The opening question and the scope note name the same subject; the question can be answered by the chapter's own content.

page_hint: Ch 15, §4 subsection heading 'Goodput vs. Batch Size: the Cache Lever' and Fig 15.2 caption
quoted_clause: #### Goodput vs. Batch Size: the Cache Lever
observed: The heading names one lever and mislabels the other. The subsection and figure cover two levers on two different phases — prefix reuse on the prefill side (left panel) and batching on the decode side (right panel) — and the prose says so explicitly ('Two distinct levers act on different phases'). The heading's 'the Cache Lever' also mislabels the right panel, which is not about caching at all.
evidence: Fig 15.2 caption: 'Two levers, two serving phases: prefix caching cuts prefill work per repeated prompt (left)... batching raises decode goodput (right...)'.
correction: Retitle: '#### Two levers: prefix reuse (prefill) and batching (decode)'.
acceptance_test: The subsection heading names both levers the subsection discusses and does not label the decode panel as caching.

quoted_clause: the ∼20 % affinity throughput gain and the ∼2.1 s cold-start warm‑up cost are themselves [ILLUSTRATIVE SCENARIO RESULT] values, not measured results.
observed: §4 explicitly distinguishes 'cold-start KV warm-up' (populating KV blocks for a new context) from 'model-weight loading' (streaming 140 GB into HBM) and from CUDA/JIT warm-up. The mini-case's 'cold-start warm-up' does not say which it means, and 2.1 s is only plausible for the KV-warm-up reading (a 9,500-token prefill is ~1.08 s in the canonical model); it would be implausible for 140 GB of weight loading from any non-HBM source. The chapter sets up the distinction and then fails to apply it.
evidence: §4: '"cold-start KV warm-up" (populating the KV-cache blocks for a new context) is different from "model-weight loading" (streaming the 140 GB weights into HBM)'. §8: 'the ∼2.1 s cold-start warm-up cost'.
correction: Name it: 'the ∼2.1 s cold-start KV warm-up (populating the KV blocks for a 9,500-token context), distinct from model-weight loading (§4)'.
acceptance_test: The mini-case's cold-start figure names which warm-up it refers to, consistent with §4's distinction; no reader can mistake it for a weight-loading time.

quoted_clause: [UNMEASURED]
observed: The book's evidence-label vocabulary (defined in Ch 4 and the Appendix A axis table) is provenance [1P] [2-degree] [LAB] [ILLUSTRATIVE] and status [FACT] [DERIVED] [ASSUMPTION] [HYPOTHESIS] [UNRESOLVED], plus [ANALYTICAL]. '[UNMEASURED]' is a member of neither axis. In this instance it is being used to mark a label quoted from Ch 14 ('hypothetical, not a measurement made for this book'), which is a different thing from the book's own label — but the typography makes it indistinguishable from one.
evidence: The surrounding sentence already quotes Ch 14's wording in quotation marks; the bracketed [UNMEASURED] then adds a second, non-vocabulary marker.
correction: Either add [UNMEASURED] to the Appendix A axis table as a status value if it is intended as a book-wide label, or render it as part of the quotation (e.g. 'Ch 14 labels this "hypothetical, not a measurement made for this book"') so that no non-vocabulary bracket appears in the book's own voice.
acceptance_test: Every bracketed label in Ch 15 appears in the Appendix A axis table, or is visibly a quotation of another chapter's wording.

page_hint: Ch 16, §2 Mental Model, second bullet ('Follow the token, not the GPU')
quoted_clause: Two systems with the same card count can differ 10× in cost per request if one has 3× the goodput per card, better utilization, or no idle coasting.
observed: The stated magnitude does not follow from the stated mechanism. Three times the goodput per card yields three times lower cost per request, not ten times. The 'or' list implies compounding factors without showing the composition, in a section whose stated purpose is to 'keep the arithmetic honest'.
evidence: cost per request ∝ (cost per card-hour) / (goodput per card-hour). A 3× goodput improvement alone gives a 3× cost reduction. Reaching 10× requires roughly 3× goodput × ~3× utilization, which the sentence does not state.
correction: Either show the composition explicitly ('3× the goodput per card and 3× the utilization gives ≈9× lower cost per request, before removing idle coasting') or restate as 'can differ several-fold'.
acceptance_test: The numeric claim is reproducible from the factors printed beside it, or the number is removed.

quoted_clause: The decision shape is a **break-even graph**: at low volume, managed/cloud‑and‑shut‑down wins (no idle capex); at high volume, self‑hosted cards amortize below the per‑token rate.
observed: The chapter's stated purpose is that '"we save money by self-hosting" is either proven or refuted by arithmetic', yet the Mental Model section states the expected conclusion as a general fact, before the arithmetic, and without the conditions that make it true (achievable utilization, staffing amortized over volume, quality parity with the API, and the prevailing API price level). The conclusion is workload- and market-dependent, and the book elsewhere insists on scoping such claims.
evidence: Chapter opening: 'After this chapter, "we save money by self-hosting" is either proven or refuted by arithmetic, and the break-even point between modes is explicit.'
correction: Hedge and state the conditions where the conclusion is first asserted: 'in the canonical regime, and provided utilization, staffing and quality-parity assumptions hold, the expected shape is ...; the crossover point is what we compute.'
acceptance_test: The conditions attached to the break-even shape are stated where it is first asserted, and the worked example either confirms or refutes it rather than restating it.

page_hint: Ch 16 — 'Mode 2 — cloud GPU instances (rent, occupancy-input priced)', 'Default paid-occupancy ASSUMPTION' paragraph; also Table 16-1 row 'B. Cloud, default paid-occupancy input'; also 'Reading the result' paragraph. Page not determinable from chunk.
quoted_clause: The canonical default bills **6 × 730 = 4,380 host-hours → $87,600/month → $14.04 per 1,000 requests** (14.038461538461538 exact). This is an explicit illustrative occupancy INPUT: it is **not a measured duty cycle, not a load-duration integral, not a guaranteed lower bound, not a complete warm-plus-burst forecast, and not a proven feasible serving schedule**
observed: The default cloud occupancy input bills exactly 6 hosts for the entire month. The chapter's own screens make 6 hosts the *average* (10 rps) requirement and 21 hosts the *peak* (40 rps) requirement; the per-host admitted-rate ceiling is C/W = 17/8.6 = 1.9767 req/s, so 6 hosts can admit at most 6 × 1.9767 ≈ 11.9 req/s — under one third of the canonical 40 rps peak. The chapter never states this arithmetic. Its caveats describe the input as 'unmeasured' and 'not a proven feasible serving schedule', which understates the defect: the configuration is not merely unmeasured, it is arithmetically incapable of serving the stated peak. The $14.04/1K line is nevertheless the default row of Table 16-1, the basis of the '~1.8' self-host-to-cloud ratio, and the line the 'When each wins' section uses to say cloud wins.
evidence: 6 × 1.9767 = 11.86 req/s < 40 rps peak. The chapter's own mid-case example ('~6 reserved warm hosts + ~15 burst hosts held for ~4 peak hours/day') confirms that the 4,380 host-hour default is the warm pool only, with no burst term. The chapter's mid-case arithmetic (6 × 730 × $20 + 15 × 4 h × 30 d × $20 = $87,600 + $36,000 = $123,600) sits between the two named endpoints, confirming the default omits the burst.
root_cause: The occupancy input was chosen as 'the average host count' without checking it against the peak requirement, and the caveat language was written to cover 'unmeasured' rather than 'infeasible'. The gap then propagates into the headline ratio and the mode-ranking prose.
correction: State the arithmetic in the Default paid-occupancy ASSUMPTION paragraph and in Table 16-1's status cell: '6 hosts × 1.9767 req/s ≈ 11.9 rps < the canonical 40 rps peak — this configuration cannot serve the canonical peak; it is priced only as a lower-bound occupancy illustration.' Then either relabel the row 'B₀ — occupancy input, peak-infeasible (lower bound only)' and add the burst term to the default, or keep the row and add a sentence in 'Reading the result' that the $14.04/1K line is not a serviceable configuration for the canonical workload and cannot be read as 'cloud is cheaper at 6.24M'.
acceptance_test: The rendered text contains the inequality 6 × 1.9767 ≈ 11.9 rps < 40 rps adjacent to the $87,600 figure; Table 16-1's status cell for that row states the configuration is peak-infeasible; and the 'Reading the result' paragraph no longer presents $14.04/1K as a comparable alternative without that qualifier.

page_hint: Ch 16 — opening ('Size the fleet first, then price it'); the sizing-screen table; 'Parametric sensitivity is the durable form', bullet 'Fleet size'.
quoted_clause: We therefore size the fleet first (Ch 17) and price it second. … **Independent prefill screen — case (ii) full-square conservative** (×1.1723 on case (i)) … so **which FLOP-counting case is stated decides whether the compute screen (19), the KV screen (21), or the compute screen again (22) governs the peak**
observed: Chapter 16 prices a fleet whose sizing method is taught in Ch 17 and Ch 20 — later in the book. The chapter's central sensitivity (21 vs 22 hosts) is explicitly conditioned on three FLOP-counting cases — (i) linear-only, (ii) full-square conservative, (iii) causal-triangle — that are never defined, described, or sourced in this chapter; only their multipliers (×1.0861, ×1.1723) are given. A reader arriving at Ch 16 cannot evaluate which case is appropriate and therefore cannot judge the headline host count, even though the chapter tells them the choice 'decides' the answer.
evidence: The three case names appear only as labels; no definition of 'linear-only', 'full-square', or 'causal-triangle' appears anywhere in the chunk. The chapter's own framing ('size the fleet first (Ch 17) and price it second') is a rhetorical ordering that contradicts the book's physical ordering.

correction: Either (a) move Ch 16 after Ch 17 (and Ch 20) so the sizing method precedes the pricing, or (b) add a short boxed gloss immediately before the sizing table defining the three cases in one sentence each — what each adds to the FLOP count, its multiplier, and which is conservative — with a forward pointer to Ch 17/20 for the derivation. Keep the 'size first, then price' framing either way, but make the reader able to evaluate the case choice.
acceptance_test: A reader who has not yet read Ch 17 can state, from Ch 16 alone, what distinguishes cases (i), (ii) and (iii) and why the peak host count is 21 under (i)/(iii) and 22 under (ii); no forward reference in Ch 16 points to material that Ch 16 has not already stated.

page_hint: Ch 16 — 'Mode 3 — managed inference API' cost equation; the 'Independent prefill screen' rows of the sizing table; the floor-17 KV computation in 'Step 1 — fleet size'.
observed: The chapter never states the canonical request's token composition. Three screens depend on it and each uses a different total: the KV screen uses 9,500 tokens/request, the prefill screen charges 9,200 tokens/request, and the API cost line uses 9,200 input + 300 output. The chunk's internal evidence is consistent with a 9,200-token prompt plus 300 generated tokens (a 'prefill' screen that charges 9,200 tokens/request; a 1.08 s prefill / 7.5 s decode split implying ~8,500 tok/s prefill and ~40 tok/s decode; 9,500 = 9,200 + 300). But the book's canonical workload is also described elsewhere as 1,200 + 8,000 = 9,200 tokens, under which the API line would be 0.002 × 1.2 + 0.008 × 8.0 = $0.0664/request — a 3.2× swing that reverses the chapter's 'self-host sits above the API at 6.24M' conclusion and moves the API break-even from ~7.5M to ~2.35M. The reader cannot resolve this from the chapter.
evidence: 0.002 × 1.2 + 0.008 × 8.0 = 0.0024 + 0.064 = $0.0664/req → $66.4/1K → 6.24M × 0.0664 = $414,336/mo; 155,816.93 / 0.0664 = 2,346,637 req/mo. Under the 9,200/300 reading the printed $0.0208 is correct. The chapter supplies no statement of I and O in tokens, so neither reading can be confirmed from the text.
root_cause: The chapter borrows canonical token counts from Ch 4/Ch 17 without restating the split, and the API line is the only place in the chapter where the input/output split changes the answer by more than 3×.
correction: State the canonical request shape explicitly in this chapter (e.g. 'the canonical request carries a 9,200-token prompt and generates 300 tokens; 9,500 tokens of KV per request'), and annotate the API equation with 'I = 9,200 tokens, O = 300 tokens'. Reconcile against design/canonical-workload.yaml; if the canonical is in fact 1,200 in / 8,000 out, recompute the API line, the $129,792/mo figure, the $20.8/1K cell, the $15–25/1K band and every break-even in the chapter.
acceptance_test: The chapter states I and O in tokens next to the API equation and the stated split matches design/canonical-workload.yaml and the 9,500-token KV figure; a reader can recompute $0.0208/request from the stated I, O and prices without consulting another chapter.

page_hint: Ch 16 — sizing-screen table, rows 'Independent prefill screen — case (i)/(ii)/(iii)'.
quoted_clause: **Independent prefill screen — case (ii) full-square conservative** (×1.1723 on case (i)) | 6 hosts | 22 hosts
observed: The case (ii) peak cell (22) cannot be reproduced from the table's own displayed values: the case (i) peak cell shows 19 hosts, and 19 × 1.1723 = 22.27 → ⌈22.27⌉ = 23, not 22. The multipliers are in fact applied to the unrounded 368,000/19,780 = 18.606 (18.606 × 1.1723 = 21.81 → 22), which the prose states only once, much later, and only for case (ii) — not for case (iii).

correction: Put the unrounded value in the table cells — e.g. '18.606 → ×1.0861 → 20.21 → 21' and '18.606 → ×1.1723 → 21.81 → 22' — and state once, above the table, that the multipliers apply to the unrounded case (i) value.

page_hint: Ch 16 — 'Treat both provisioning policies explicitly' paragraph; provisioning-policy table, last column.
quoted_clause: The capacity-planning rule (Ch 17's authoritative provisioning-policy table, **Table 17-1**) is N = ⌈λ·W/(C·u·ρ)⌉ + N_spare with u = 0.70 and ρ = 0.95 **independent** (u × ρ = 0.665, not nested) … at the 70% × 95% + N−1 policy case (ii) gives **⌈21.81/0.665⌉ + 1 = 34 hosts** against **32** for KV-only
observed: u = 0.70 is a KV-slot occupancy target and ρ = 0.95 a scheduling factor; the formula's denominator C is a slot count. The 34-host row applies the same ÷0.665 derate to the case (ii) *compute* screen, whose 'C' is a token rate (19,780 tok/s/host), not a slot count. page_hint: Ch 16 — 'Parametric multi-region worksheet' table, rows 2, 3 and 8.

quoted_clause: **Break-even volume** — the requests/month where self-host cost-per-request crosses managed API; below it, don't buy cards.

The rule also compares only against the managed API, while the cloud alternative ($87,600/mo) lies below the flat self-host line ($155,816.93/mo) at every volume — so on the chapter's own numbers self-host never wins against cloud, at any volume.
evidence: Mini-case: break-even $40,000 ÷ $0.0208 = 1,923,077 ≈ 1.9M; volume 5M = 2.6× that; verdict 'start on the managed API now'. Cloud $87,600 < API $129,792 < self-host $155,816.93 at 6.24M req/mo, and the self-host line is flat in volume.
root_cause: A necessary condition was promoted to a decision rule; the chapter's own conclusion contradicts it and the rule silently omits the third comparator.
correction: Restate metric 3 as necessary-but-not-sufficient: 'break-even against the managed API is a necessary condition for self-hosting to be cheaper on price alone; it is not sufficient — the staff/ops and opportunity-cost terms, the cloud alternative, and the availability scope can still favour the API (see §8).'
acceptance_test: No passage asserts that volume above break-even implies self-hosting; §4 metric 3 and §8's verdict are mutually consistent.

page_hint: Ch 16 §8 mini-case (staff-basis paragraph); affects §6 headline break-even and Fig 16.1
quoted_clause: not Mode 1's mature-operator alloc (~$10K/mo for 21 hosts)
observed: The canonical self-host line's staff term is $10,000/mo for 21 hosts (168 GPUs). At the mini-case's own fully-loaded rate ($624K/yr per FTE = $52K/mo), $10,000/mo buys 0.19 FTE — about 1 FTE per 5.3 hosts — versus the mini-case's 0.25 FTE per host, a 27× difference in staffing intensity. §4 metric 4 says the staff term 'dominates the comparisons', yet the headline break-even (~7.5M) is quoted as a point with no sensitivity to it, and the two staffing bases are never reconciled.
evidence: Independent derivation of the canonical staff term: the 21→22 host delta ($162,760.59 − $155,816.93 = $6,943.66/mo) is the per-host capex+energy; $155,816.93 − 21 × $6,943.66 = $10,000.07/mo staff, confirming the $10K figure from a second direction. At $52K/mo per FTE that is 0.19 FTE for 168 GPUs. Re-pricing at 1 FTE per 8 hosts (2.6 FTE, $137K/mo) gives self-host ≈ $282,817/mo and break-even ≈ 13.6M req/mo; at the mini-case's 0.25 FTE/host (5.25 FTE, $273K/mo) break-even ≈ 20.1M req/mo.
root_cause: Two staffing bases coexist in one chapter (canonical $10K/mo vs mini-case $26K/mo for 0.5 FTE); the canonical's is never checked against the chapter's own fully-loaded rate, and the break-even is presented as a point rather than as a function of the staff term.
correction: State the canonical staffing model explicitly (FTE per N hosts, or hours per host per week), reconcile it with the mini-case's $624K/yr fully-loaded rate, and add a one-line sensitivity of the break-even to the staff term (e.g., 'at 1 FTE per 8 hosts the break-even rises to ~13.6M req/mo').
acceptance_test: The canonical staff term is stated as a derived quantity with its FTE basis, and the break-even is presented with at least one alternative-staffing value.

page_hint: Ch 16 Note 16.1-1 (feasible bound), Fig 16.1 caption and figure spec, §6
quoted_clause: The feasible served-volume bound (40 rps × 624,000 canonical active s ≈ 24.96M req/mo) and the shaded infeasible band right of it
observed: The bound is a property of the canonical demand shape (business hours), not of the fleet. The fleet's capacity is ~40 rps; a 24×7 workload could serve 40 rps × 2,592,000 s ≈ 103.7M req/mo on the same hardware. The chapter's own mini-case uses a 24×7 shape (2.5M active s/mo, 4× the canonical), so the shaded region is not infeasible in general — only unreachable by the canonical shape. Labelling it 'infeasible' invites the reader to conclude a hard capacity ceiling.
evidence: Mini-case: 5M req/mo at 2 rps = 2,500,000 active s/mo vs canonical 624,000 s/mo. 40 rps × 2,592,000 s/mo = 103.68M req/mo. Separately, 24.96M (40 rps × 624,000 s) sits close to 25.92M (10 rps × 2,592,000 s — the canonical average rate sustained 24×7); if both appear in the book they need explicit disambiguation.
root_cause: A demand-shape-derived envelope was labelled as a capacity feasibility limit; the duty-cycle assumption was carried in the formula but not in the label.
correction: Relabel the bound and the shaded band as duty-cycle-conditional: 'canonical duty-cycle envelope (40 rps × 624,000 active s/mo = 24.96M req/mo)'; state that a 24×7 shape raises the envelope to ~103.7M req/mo on the same fleet; and print the formula next to the number so it cannot be confused with 25.92M.
acceptance_test: No figure, caption or note labels a region 'infeasible' without naming the duty-cycle assumption that makes it so; the bound's formula appears adjacent to its value.

quoted_clause: **cloud** = 4,380 paid host-hours (6 × 730) — a single occupancy INPUT priced against the canonical 6.24M req/mo, so it is drawn as a **marker at that one priced operating point**
observed: The cloud marker is 6 hosts against the self-host fleet's 21 hosts — 3.5× fewer GPUs if the host types match — and it is the lowest point on the chart at the canonical volume, yet the figure's Takeaway compares only self-host vs API and never states the ordering of all three. The caption's scope caveat says the modes are 'not compared on matched availability/SLO/warm-capacity assumptions' but never quantifies the capacity gap, so a reader can take the $87.6K marker as a like-for-like winner.
evidence: 21 hosts × 8 GPUs = 168 GPUs vs 6 × 8 = 48 GPUs. At 6.24M req/mo: cloud $87,600 < API $129,792 < self-host $155,816.93.
root_cause: The scope mismatch is disclosed in general terms but not quantified, and the Takeaway line omits the cheapest plotted point.
correction: State the cloud configuration's GPU count and its peak capacity relative to the 21-host fleet; add to the Takeaway that the cloud marker is the lowest plotted point but is not capacity-matched, and that equalizing scope is expected to raise it.
acceptance_test: Fig 16.1's caption states the cloud fleet's GPU count and capacity ratio to the self-host fleet, and the Takeaway names all three modes at the canonical volume.

quoted_clause: self-host wins only once volume passes the ~7.5M break-even — lower if the staff/ops term is sunk — with sustained near-peak utilization and a benchmark confirming the SLO
observed: At the break-even volume the fleet is nowhere near peak: 7.49M req/mo ÷ 624,000 active s = 12.0 rps against a 40 rps peak, i.e. 30% of peak. The canonical workload's own shape is 10 rps average = 25% of peak. The stated condition 'sustained near-peak utilization' is therefore not met by the workload the chapter analyses and cannot be met at the volume where the crossover occurs.
root_cause: The condition was written from intuition about fixed-cost economics rather than from the chapter's own rps arithmetic.
correction: Replace with the computed condition: 'with the fleet running at ~12 rps of its 40 rps peak (30%) at the crossover — i.e. the fixed-cost advantage is won with substantial idle capacity, which is why this is a frozen-fleet crossover, not a scalable one'.
acceptance_test: The utilization condition in §6 is stated in rps or as a percentage of the 40 rps peak and is consistent with the 12 rps implied by the break-even volume.

quoted_clause: **Effective utilization** — actual goodput ÷ theoretical capacity across the billing period
observed: The numerator is SLO-qualified (goodput) and the denominator is not (theoretical capacity/peak). The ratio mixes two different operating points and can never approach 1 even for a fleet fully saturated at the SLO — the same peak-vs-sustained conflation the book elsewhere insists on separating. A second, different utilization definition ('served ÷ provisioned') appears in Note 16.1-1 with no cross-reference distinguishing them.
evidence: Internal: §6 distinguishes 'planning bounds' from 'a measured p95 TTFT/TPOT pass'; Note 16.1-1 defines utilization as served ÷ provisioned, which is not the §4 definition and is not labelled as a different quantity.
root_cause: Denominator population mismatch (SLO-qualified numerator against unqualified peak denominator), compounded by a second, unlabelled utilization definition in the same chapter.
correction: Define effective utilization = SLO-qualified goodput ÷ sustained SLO-qualified capacity (measured at the same SLO), and in Note 16.1-1 state explicitly that the figure's utilization is served ÷ provisioned, not the §4 effective utilization.
acceptance_test: Both utilization definitions appear with numerator and denominator stated, and the note distinguishes them by name.

quoted_clause: A startup's CTO shows the architect a warrant to buy two 8×H100 servers for the new internal RAG assistant

Mini-case: 2 hosts = 16 GPUs → 8 replicas at 2 rps average (0.25 rps/replica) — comfortably inside the canonical's demonstrated per-replica capability, but only if the topology is stated.

observed: The second-engineer branch is stated without the condition that makes it work. Hiring a second engineer adds cash cost that is not in the $40K; the branch is valid only if that engineer was already on the plan (or if the displaced product work is worth less than their cost). As written, 'a second engineer frees up' is offered as a free lever, and the closing sentence 'runs the same numbers and buys the servers' contradicts the earlier 're-run the same model'.

quoted_clause: same per-request price, a different duty cycle
observed: The mini-case inherits the canonical's blended $0.0208/request, but the canonical workload and a RAG assistant have different input/output mixes, and the chapter's own note defines the API line as input×$/1M + output×$/1M-out — linear in volume only at a fixed mix. page_hint: Ch 18 §18.3.1 table row '70B dense 8-bit'; §18.3.2 'Row hardware' parenthetical; §18.3.4 closing paragraph; §18.3.5 'The FP16 tier has no separate reserve'
quoted_clause: 70B dense 8-bit | — | ~70 GB | — | 1 (weights alone fit on 1×H100, leaving 7 GPUs; with the canonical KV budget the 8×H100 pool still holds weights + KV) ... Row hardware ... 70B dense 8-bit on 1×H100 ... routing 70% of requests to an 8-bit model on 1×H100 changes the per-host KV ceiling accordingly
observed: The chapter prices and routes 70% of traffic to a 70B 8-bit model hosted on a single H100, while simultaneously using the canonical 9,500-token request profile for the cost arithmetic. On one H100 (80 GB) the 8-bit weights consume ~70 GB, leaving ~10 GB for KV. The chapter's own canonical KV figure is kappa = 2.62 MB/token, so one canonical request needs 9,500 x 2.62 MB = 24.89 GB of KV. 10 GB < 24.89 GB, so a 1xH100 8-bit instance can hold ZERO concurrent canonical requests. The chapter states this arithmetic correctly for the FP16 tier (a 2-GPU shard holds 160 - 140 = 20 GB of KV headroom against the 24.9 GB one request needs) but never applies the same test to the tier that carries 70% of the traffic. The placement is also internally inconsistent: §18.3.1 places the 8-bit instance on the 8xH100 pool, while §18.3.2's cost basis and §18.3.4/§18.3.5 assume 1xH100.
evidence: Recomputed from the book's own constants: weights 70 GB (8-bit of 70B); H100 HBM 80 GB; free = 10 GB; canonical request KV = 9,500 tokens x 2.62 MB/token = 24.89 GB (the same number the chapter prints in §18.3.5); 10/24.89 = 0.40 requests. Minimum placement for one canonical request on the 8-bit tier = ceil((70 + 24.89)/80) = 2 GPUs (160 GB, 90 GB KV, 3 concurrent requests).

page_hint: Ch 18 §18.3.3 'Mixed-fleet hourly cost' / 'Monthly savings'; §18.3.4 final paragraph; §18.3.1 co-residency paragraph
quoted_clause: **Monthly savings** ≈ ($23.75 − $12.59) × 730 hr ≈ **$8,147 / month** (≈ 47% reduction) ... The latency and capacity must also reconcile with the canonical workload's KV residency (Chapter 17): routing 70% of requests to an 8-bit model on 1×H100 changes the per-host KV ceiling accordingly, and the fleet host count is set by the model each tier runs on.

Total in-flight at the 40 rps peak is 344 regardless of routing, so N = ceil(344/9) = 39 hosts at full utilization and ceil(344/(9 x 0.665)) = 58 at the 70% x 95% policy, versus 21 / 31 for the single-model fleet. Dropping the unrouted 4-bit tier (weights 280 GB, KV 296 GB, C = 11) still gives 32 / 48 hosts. Dedicated-host placement (one 8xH100 per tier: 8-bit and MoE-8-bit get 640 - 70 - 64 = 506 GB KV, C = 20; FP16 gets C = 17) gives 13 + 4 + 3 = 20 hosts at full utilization and 20 + 7 + 5 = 32 at the policy, i.e. roughly a wash. At ~$300-400K per 8xH100 host, the shared-pool branch adds ~18-27 hosts (~$6-11M capital) against a $8,147/month (~$98K/yr) token-cost saving.
root_cause: The chapter optimizes the numerator of cost (per-token rate) while ignoring the dominant term (host count), and never fixes the placement assumption that determines it.
correction: State the placement assumption explicitly (shared pool vs one host group per tier), compute the resulting per-tier C and the resulting N for both the single-model and the mixed fleet, and present the savings as a total-cost comparison (host amortization + energy + token cost) rather than a token-cost comparison. acceptance_test: §18.3.3 or §18.3.5 contains a host-count table for the single-model fleet and the mixed fleet under one stated placement, with the same u x rho policy as Table 17-1, and the '$8,147/month (47%)' figure is presented as one component of a total-cost comparison rather than as the saving.

page_hint: Ch 18 §18.3.2 latency column; §18.3.4 'Scope note'; §18.8 mini-case Tier 1 and the SLO check
quoted_clause: | 70B 4-bit GGUF | $0.15 | 800 | energy only | ... **Tier 1 (4-bit GGUF):** Handles 80% of queries (FAQ, account lookup). Runs on edge nodes (AMD Ryzen 7950X, 64 GB RAM). observed: The latency column is never defined as time-to-first-token or as full generation latency, and under the full-generation reading the printed values are physically impossible by roughly two orders of magnitude. A 70B 4-bit model is ~35 GB of weights; a Ryzen 7950X with dual-channel DDR5-5600 sustains roughly 70-90 GB/s, so each generated token requires streaming ~35 GB, i.e. ~0.4-0.5 s/token. A 250-token request therefore takes ~100-120 s, not 600 ms. The 600 ms and 800 ms figures are only defensible as time-to-first-token, which the chapter never says. The mini-case's central conclusion (Tier 1 violates the 500 ms SLO) is therefore reached with a number that is wrong by ~200x under the natural reading, and the 'recalculate with a feasible Tier 1' step depends on the 250 ms GPU figure being a comparable quantity.
evidence: 35 GB / ~75 GB/s = ~0.47 s per token; 250 tokens = ~117 s. The chapter's own §18.3.4 scope note says these are 'not the canonical TTFT/TPOT SLO (Ch 4)', which leaves the quantity undefined. The mini-case's SLO gate compares a per-request figure against a 500 ms per-request deadline, while §18.4 defines the fleet metric as 'p95 of token-level latency per model'.
root_cause: The latency column was populated with plausible-looking placeholder numbers without a definition of the measured quantity, and no bandwidth-bound sanity check was applied.
correction: Define the column explicitly (TTFT, or full request latency, or both) and re-derive the values. For the CPU 4-bit tier, either state TTFT (~0.5 s) and label the SLO gate as a TTFT gate, or replace the value with a defensible full-generation latency and let the mini-case's conclusion follow from the corrected number. Apply the same definition to §18.4's 'Latency p95 per model' metric so the metric and the SLO share a unit.
acceptance_test: The §18.3.2 latency column header names the quantity; every value in it is consistent with the memory-bandwidth bound for the stated hardware and request length; the §18.4 metric and the §18.8 SLO gate use the same quantity.

page_hint: Ch 18 §18.3.1 table row '70B dense FP16' and the paragraph immediately following the table

quoted_clause: *(Scope note: these tier per-token rates are illustrative scenario values that **differ from the §18.3.2 per-1M ledger** — they are not the ledger's $1.25 (8-bit) / $2.50 (FP16) / $0.15 (4-bit) per-1M rates converted, and the 4-bit tier's ~600 ms latency differs from the ledger's 800 ms. quoted_clause: **Planning-bound caveat:** these host counts are **lower bounds on the host count that derive from the KV-slot-based analytical UPPER bound on the per-host completion rate** (the direction flips once, at N = λ/(C/W)); the deployable fleet is the **maximum** of that capacity requirement and the measured tail-latency (N_SLO) requirement, not the capacity screen alone.

As printed, the stated flip point is the point at which the fleet is already 50% over the policy-adjusted ceiling. The clause also appears to be a vestige: the substantive claim (the counts are lower bounds because C/W is an upper bound on per-host completion rate; take the max with N_SLO) is correct and should stand alone.

acceptance_test: Any threshold stated in the caveat uses the same u x rho policy as the table, or the caveat contains no threshold.

quoted_clause: GPU inference time is not constant; under sustained high load, kernel‑mode preemption, memory fragmentation, and concurrent kernel launches can increase per‑token latency by 20–50%. The linear model t = t_inference + t_tool is a lower bound; the architect should add a 20% safety margin.
observed: Two problems. (1) The 20-50% degradation range is an unsourced quantitative claim about a specific set of mechanisms, presented in the same register as the book's measured or derived numbers; it carries no evidence label and no source. (2) The prescribed remedy is inconsistent with the stated range: if per-token latency can rise 20-50%, a 20% safety margin covers only the bottom of the range and leaves the architect exposed at the top. 'kernel-mode preemption' is also ambiguous - it reads as OS kernel mode rather than GPU kernel time-slicing between concurrently resident kernels.
evidence: The book's own evidence-label vocabulary (Ch 4 / Appendix A) includes [ILLUSTRATIVE], [ASSUMPTION] and [HYPOTHESIS]; this range carries none. The margin (20%) is at the minimum of the stated range (20-50%).
root_cause: A rule of thumb was written without a source and without reconciling the range with the margin.
correction: Either source the 20-50% range (a measured or published result with its workload and hardware stated) and label it accordingly, or reframe it as an [ASSUMPTION] with the mechanism named. Then make the margin consistent with the range (e.g. 'size the margin against the upper end of the range, or measure the degradation on the target deployment') and rename 'kernel-mode preemption' to 'kernel time-slicing between concurrent GPU kernels'.
acceptance_test: The 20-50% figure carries an evidence label and a source or is labeled [ASSUMPTION]; the recommended margin is at least as large as the upper end of the stated range, or the text says the margin must be set from measurement.

quoted_clause: Hardware L7 switches offer better ρ (≈0.98) but less fine‑grained traffic‑shaping; software LBs offer ρ ≈ 0.95 but can implement consistent hashing for session affinity. The architect should match the LB capability to the session model: sticky sessions → any LB; stateless → software LB with consistent hashing.
observed: The guidance is inverted. Consistent hashing is a session-affinity mechanism: it deliberately pins a key to a host. A stateless routing policy (any host may serve any request) wants least-connections or power-of-two-choices, not consistent hashing, which would reintroduce the affinity the policy is trying to avoid. The second clause also contradicts the first: if software LBs are the ones that 'can implement consistent hashing for session affinity', then 'sticky sessions -> any LB' is not true, and the hardware/software distinction the paragraph sets up is not the one that matters. The paragraph's real decision variable is whether the LB supports affinity at all, not whether it is hardware or software.
evidence: The paragraph's own premises: hardware L7 = better rho, less shaping; software = lower rho, consistent hashing. The recommendation maps sticky sessions to 'any LB' and stateless to 'consistent hashing', which inverts both premises.
root_cause: The recommendation was written from a list of LB features rather than from the routing policy each feature implements.
correction: Restate the decision as: (a) if the session model requires affinity, the LB must support it (consistent hashing or cookie/session pinning) - note that hardware L7 support varies by platform and must be verified; (b) if the session model is stateless, use least-connections or power-of-two-choices so that load follows capacity, and do not use consistent hashing. Keep the rho values as the cost of each choice, and note that the rho difference (0.98 vs 0.95) changes the host count by roughly 3% at the canonical fleet size.
acceptance_test: The recommendation for each session model names a routing algorithm consistent with that model, and no sentence recommends consistent hashing for stateless routing.

page_hint: Ch 17, Table 17-2, row 'in-flight @ agentic no-reuse W=17.70s'
quoted_clause: | in-flight @ agentic no-reuse W=17.70s | 708 | 1,770 | 3,541 |
observed: The row is not internally consistent with its own multiplier: 708 x 2 = 1,416 and 1,770 x 2 = 3,540, not 3,541. The 3,541 comes from rounding 200 x 17.7032 s up, while the 1,770 in the same row comes from rounding 100 x 17.7032 s down. The inconsistency is harmless to the derived host counts (both 3,540 and 3,541 give ceil(./8.645) = 410) but it is visible in the row and will be read as an arithmetic error.

correction: Use one rounding rule for the row (e.g. 708 / 1,770 / 3,540 from the displayed W = 17.70 s, or 708 / 1,770 / 3,541 from the unrounded W with a note), and state which.

quoted_clause: In the canonical scenario with φ = 0.1, λ = 40 rps, D = 5 MB ... With the illustrative φ = 0.05 and D = 5 MB, the network rule must also use the new 100-rps traffic
observed: The cross-host fraction phi changes from 0.1 in §17.6 to 0.05 in §17.8 with no stated reason. Both are labeled illustrative, but the reader is given no basis for the change and no indication that the two are meant to describe different deployments. Since phi is the parameter that decides whether the fabric is a real constraint, the change should be explained (e.g. 'the agentic layer adds local tool calls, so the cross-host fraction halves') or held constant.
root_cause: The mini-case was written with its own scenario parameters without reconciling them with the chapter's canonical scenario.
